subtopic: FACILITIES OF PACIFIC COAST COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction? Can the facilities of the Pacific coast communications system, recently declared surplus to requirements by the armed forces, now be made available for use by the general public?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
subtopic: FACILITIES OF PACIFIC COAST COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM
speechtext: War Assets are now dealing with the property in question. It will take some time before arrangements can be made to place the services under civilian ownership or to operate them under civilian control. Until then, it will not be possible to throw the facilities open to public use. The services are not willing to open the service to the public, and as long as they are operating the facilities, nothing can be done.

The house resumed from Wednesday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fernand Viau for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.
Would the hon. member permit a correction?
I should be very happy to.

He has
omitted the cost of manufacturing of the 9% pounds of cheese in 100 pounds of milk, at
the rate of 2% cents, which would be subtracted from the price received by the producer. This does not apply to butter. Furthermore, the hon. member has not referred to the value of skim milk in the feeding of young cattle and poultry, which amounts to about 40 cents per hundred pounds.

I am very grateful to the hon. member for his observations. However I think the Chair will admit the hon. member did not ask a question. I concede readily that the feeding value of skim milk is greater than that of whey, and that calves or pigs fed on whey would not fatten for the market. As against that however there is the labour charge for separating the milk and washing the machine; all those dreary hours of drudgery that are completely eliminated when the whole milk, as it comes from the cow, is sold to the cheese factory.

It is the
same thing if one takes milk to the cheese factory.

My hon. friend has not asked a question; I submit with great deference that the additional labour the butter producer has to put into his product offsets added value that may be found in buttermilk when compared with whey.
To pursue further my earlier observations:
I said it was easy to understand why the minister should seek to retain a high and ranking place for Canadian cheese in the British market. Our butter making is not considered a success in Great Britain; whether our butter be good or bad is beside the issue. We do not make the kind of butter that is liked in England. We do not make butter which competes successfully in the English market with Irish butter, Danish butter, or with that commodity about which we heard so much in other times and places-New Zealand butter. On the other hand Canadian cheese is so highly esteemed in Great Britain that they call it English Stilton. It is consumed in large quantities, and undoubtedly if that market could be secured for us in perpetuity, and without rivalry, it would be beneficial to the Canadian producer.
I submit, however, that that market must not be secured at the cost of an injustice and of permanent damage to the dairy industry as a whole, and to the dairy industry of Southeastern Quebec in particular. Canadians are a butter-eating people; the eating of butter is a life habit. I do not believe it is a habit from which they can be easily weaned. To-day it is practically impossible to buy butter. We find that the reserves stand at roughly 9 million pounds, whereas
The Address-Mr. Hackett

a year ago they were 20 million, two years ago about the same figure, and for the last five years at this time of year they have shown an average of about 18 million pounds plus. '	*
I speak only of creamery butter, of course. To-day our reserves in creameries, storage and transit are barely' 9 million pounds, or less than half of what .they were a y'ear ago, or what they have * been on the average in the last five years. I point this out to show that there is a scarcity.
I wish to put on record the following table to show the number of dairy cattle exported to the United States in (the past ten years:

Those are the numbers of dairy cattle exported to the United States under a system of price fixing, controls and inadequate returns to the makers of butter, and during the four year period which preceded the war. The number exported has increased over threefold during the period of controls. The number exported to the United States this year up to March 31 is nearly double the number that was exported during the same period last year.
I want to open a parenthesis here, because one can never talk about a matter of this kind without being charged with being actuated by political considerations. I want to say that despite what has happened there was an increase of 7-2 per cent last year in the production of butter in the province of Quebec, while there was a reduction of 3-4 per cent in the production of chee-se. There is a reason for the trend. As I said a few minutes ago, the province of Ontario has paid a bonus of two cents per pound on all cheese manufactured in the province. The province of Quebec also paid a bonus on cheese. It has now ceased to pay that bonus. I cannot say whether the bonus was effective throughout the year 1945; it may have been paid until the end of the year, but it was known that the bonus on cheese was to be withdrawn, and there was an effort made by the farmers to get away from cheese production. This may explain the increase in butter production that has taken place in Quebec.
More butter is produced in Quebec than in any other province in the dominion. Quebec is essentially a butter-producing province.

Quebec hopes, and I trust not entirely in vain, that we are approaching an era when prices will cease to be fixed, when these controls will be released and when competition and orderly and unrestricted marketing will again be the vogue. The farmers of Quebec hope that the excellence of their product will bring them a decent return for their efforts.
Having stated these facts I wish to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and to the government that the ceiling price of butter be increased. I need not tell the minister that I believe that price-fixing of commodities has ceased to be useful. I believe it is baneful at the present time and I believe the Canadian farmer, particularly the Canadian dairyman, would be better off if he were freed from all restrictions and were able to enter a market in which he could buy and sell without restriction. But those ideal conditions do not yet obtain, and I am suggesting to the minister and to the government that the necessary changes be made in these ceiling prices to give the butter producer a fair return for his effort. At the present time the producer of butter is not receiving an equitable return for his product as compared with the producer of cheese. The producer of butter is not receiving a price which enables him to hire people to work for him.
Why do you not pay wages in Quebec?
We are able to carry on our dairying industry in Quebec because our families are closely knit together and because the people there are not ashamed to work.
For nothing.
The wife and daughter and the son of the household are proud and willing to go into the barnyard to help the father milk the cows and do the other chores incidental to farm life.
They do that in all parts of Canada.

I ask the minister to
take these facts into consideration and to raise the price of butter, not just four cents as was suggested in one of the papers this morning. Twenty-cent cheese means sixty-cent butter. There is no reason why that price should not be paid pending the removal of ceiling prices.
I speak for an area the population of which is fifty per cent engaged in farming and fifty per cent engaged in industry. In other words, one-half the population of these eastern counties of which I speak are makers of butter while the other half are consumers

The Address-Mr. Hackett
of butter. I believe the purchasers realize that the farmer should have a fair return for his commodity. They realize, moreover, that if he does not get a fair return, butter *will become still more scarce. Butter is becoming scarce by reason of the dissipation and sale and export of the herds. Laudable as may be the minister's desire to win and keep the cheese market of Great Britain, I suggest that he should not do that by depriving the Canadian people of butter. They will have butter, and if it cannot be made in this country, they will import it.
I noticed this morning that in another place an hon. gentleman whose political faith is identical with that of the government in power-*
Oh, no, it is not.

*-and who is not unfriendly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), brought in a bill under the heading "Dairy Industry" and told his house that he was seeking to amend the Dairy Industry Act whereby certain portions of that act which prohibited the manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine in Canada would be repealed. Now if it is government policy to force Canadians to eat oleomargarine-
Who said it was?
Keep quiet, Sir Oleo.

-that it may export
cheese to Britain, I fear that the government will have to amend its policy or it will find itself with abundant leisure to think of other things. The Canadian people have a taste for butter.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the manufacture or sale of oleomargarine has never been discussed by the government at any time to my knowledge within the ten years that I have been in the government. The present law was passed I think in 1922 and has remained that way ever since. It was brought in by the then Liberal government.

My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has made a statement but it is just possible that he is not entirely aware of all that is taking place within his party. The fact remains that there has been introduced by an outstanding member of his party in the upper house a bill to repeal those portions of the Dairy Industry Act which make it illegal to import oleomargarine into Canhda at a time when there is the greatest scarcity of butter that this country has ever known, and if that bill is not intro-63260-22
duced for the purpose of substituting oleo-mhrgarine for butter, then I do not understand that twice two makes four.
I am sure that my hon. friend does not want to have a misrepresentation go out.
If my hon, friend wishes to ask a question I am willing to answer, but I have heard a number of interruptions and-

If I may ask my hon. friend a question, does he know that the Prime Minister announced this morning to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that the question had never been discussed by the government, and that the introduction of the measure referred to in the senate has nothing to do with government policy?
Hear, hear.
I was not aware of that, and I think it is unfortunate that-

,1 must ask hon. members to keep order. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has the floor, and hon. members have no right to interrupt him unless he permits a question to be asked. I hope that he will be given attention and will not be interrupted while he is speaking.
He is touching a sensitive spot. That is why he is interrupted.

When hon. gentlemen on the other side become restless and begin to find their seats uncomfortable it is perhaps because they are being told things which remind them of past errors of policy and of the retribution, swift and inexorable, which followed.
The purpose of my remarks is to ask the Minister of Agriculture to raise the ceiling price of butter so that the owners of herds can continue to make butter and that they may have from the proceeds of the sale 'of that butter money sufficient to buy the' feed that is necessary to exploit their herds, money sufficient to clothe their children properly and send them to school, money sufficient to enable them to keep their herds instead of selling them, as they have been forced to do and are doing at an alarming rate.
The market in Britain is a good market, and I commend the minister for trying to secure it for Canada. But he can secure it only if he proceeds fairly, and he cannot be unfair to a considerable element of the agricultural population and hope to bring a benefit to the rest of Canada. If he destroys the butter-making element he will weaken the

The Address-Mr. Johnston

very industry that he is seeking to strengthen. If he permits the butter maker of Quebec to be squeezed out of existence, and forty cents a pound butter is doing it, he is' following a policy which is dangerous not only to the largest single element in our country, the farming element, but to the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put I wish to say a few words. It had not been my intention earlier in this debate to take part in it but rather to leave what I had to say to another occasion.
Leave it.

I heard somebody say "Leave it". The leaders of all the parties agreed to do that very thing, but every party except the Social Credit party broke that agreement, and some to a greater degree than others. I think the greatest betrayal of that agreement was by the Conservative party, but the Liberals shared in it, and now I see they are applauding themselves. But that is not the point of my argument this afternoon. I want to deal with several matters, and I am glad the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) is in his seat, because later I shall address some remarks particularly to him.
First of all I wish to warn the house of the gradually increasing number of unemployed throughout Canada. Particularly is this so in the part of the country I come from, the west. Just before I left Calgary the unemployment register roll in that city was well nigh the 5,000 mark-and this represented people who were registered as unemployed, not counting the vast numbers of unemployed of whom there was no record. The same is true of Edmonton and of all the other cities in the west; in fact there are thousands of unemployed throughout the country, and this at a time when Canada's government is boasting that it is doing so much in an all-out production effort.
It is only a matter of months now since we had everyone employed. True, they were wearing uniforms, but the government promised them that no time would be lost in converting from war-time to peace-time production. I saw in the papers not long ago that the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) had stated it would be only a few weeks until we would be again short of man-power. I fancy he will have to do a good deal of miraculous work and planning if he expects

to be able to take up the great lag in unemployment which is increasing so rapidly across Canada.
Not only is this true among the civilian workers in war production plants who have been laid off and are now finding it impossible to get any jobs, but it is true of the veterans themselves. Many veterans in Calgary have come to me appealing for jobs, but I do not know where there are any jobs to be got. We cannot find them.
There are lots of farm jobs.
Yes, but some of you farmers, not all I am glad'to say, hardly pay help sufficient to maintain what might be called a decent standard of living.
You cannot get men at $100 a month to-day.

I do not know many who would refuse $100 a month. But that does not solve the problem of the increasing number of unemployed, and it was the hon. gentleman's party who went about the country hanging up great yellow posters-yes, they were yellow-on every telephone pole saying, "Jobs for all", and they were going to maintain the standard of pay which prevailed during the war years. The responsibility rests upon the Liberal party and other parties who advocated jobs for all. Let me tell the hon. member that it was the Social Credit party alone who told the people definitely, although it was not a popular thing to say at election time, that we knew there would not be jobs for all under the present set-up. There is no guessing about this. The facts are there; they speak for themselves. I have the posters upstairs in my desk.
One other thing which I think should be called to the attention of the government is the ever-increasing burden of taxes and the cost of living. We members in the house- and I make no apology for this, nor did I apologize for it anywhere in my constituency -voted ourselves an increase of $2,000. When I was asked about it in my constituency I made no bones about it at all. I told the people that I was one of those who did vote for the increase. It has been our policy as Social Crediters, ever since we have been in the house, to do everything possible to increase the standard of living of every Canadian. We have persistently and consistently throughout the years fought for increased living standards for all, and when we ourselves had the opportunity to give ourselves an increase-and some of us really needed it-we voted for it. It behooves every

The Address-Mr. Johnston
member of the house, therefore, to see to it, and at this session is the opportune time, that other people in Canada, especially those in the low income brackets, have some relief from the present tremendous taxation.
I suggest, and it has been suggested by other members of our party as well as members in other parts of the house, that the income tax exemption be $2,000 for married persons and $1,200 for single. That would be a step in the right direction.
The government seems to have forgotten that agricultural workers are the backbone of industry in this country. During the war years, however, the farmers have not shared in the profits which other industries have enjoyed. Indeed, they shared very little in increased prices until quite recently, and now the government comes along, when there is a chance for agriculture to participate in some small measure in any advantages there may be, and deliberately increases the cost of production by adding another cost in the price of gasoline. The farmers in my constituency are greatly perturbed by the increased cost of gasoline and white products generally, because, without any question, that raises the cost of production for the farmer. When they look across the border and see that the farmer there can purchase machinery at prices considerably less than those charged for the same machinery in Canada, made by the same companies and distributed by their agents in this country; when they see that our people have to pay twice the price, our farmers do not feel well about it. One cannot wonder at their uneasiness.
It has been suggested by the members of this party and by others that the government remove that three per cent war tax on gasoline. That would bring the price down for the benefit not only of farmers in the west but of the people generally throughout Canada. It would be 'a step in the right direction. I have here a resolution which I should like to put on the record because I know that many other members have received similar resolutions. It will give the house and the people of eastern Canada some idea of what the farmers of the west have to contend with in the way of increased costs of production. A copy of this resolution was sent to the Prime Minister:
Whereas there is to be an increase of two cents a gallon on the price of gasoline, effective March 18, 1946, and
Whereas this action on the part of the federal government will affect the farmers of Alberta in their cost of production and also the cost in all other services rendered by business _ to the farmer throughout the country, which will ultimately result in a further increased cost to the primary producer, and
Whereas we do believe the remedy could be effected in the removal of the federal tax of three cents.
Therefore the Langdon, Alberta, farmers union and the Langdon United Farmers of Alberta at a recent meeting held
Resolved that a fact-finding board be set up by federal and provincial governments to investigate into records of all oil producers, manufacturers and distributors of white products to determine whether any increase in price is justified at this time.
I think there is a great deal of merit in that resolution. A fact-finding board should be set up, in the form of a commission, to find out whether it is necessary to have increased prices in gasoline. The meeting referred to in the resolution was no small affair. There were delegates from all parts of the district. There were over 92 persons present, and the resolution represents not the feeling of a local community but the feeling of quite a large area. And the same feeling prevails generally throughout Canada.
I stated a little while ago that I should have a few words to say to the Minister of Veterans, Affairs. May I say that the minister has been very considerate in regard to conditions affecting the returned man. He has done about as good a job as any Liberal could do; in fact he is about as good a Liberal as there is.
I wish to refer to the general housing situation. Quite a few members have spoken about housing, but not from the point of view to which I wish to address myself. It has been pointed out that the housing situation is becoming desperate across the country. We all know that. When Wiartime Housing first started two or three years ago I spoke on this question because I visited Wartime Housing in Hull, and afterwards I spoke in the house with regard to things I had actually seen. Under Wartime Housing, houses were built in Hull which were a shame and a disgrace and a waste of public money. On that occasion I pointed out to the house that I had seen several 'houses in Hull the outside walls of which were falling away from the foundation. You could stick your hand between the inside partition in the house and the outside wall. I pointed that out because I had actually seen it in many houses in that city. The floors had warped to such an extent that you could not get in through the kitchen door from the outside. The door could not be opened. There was hardly a door in the whole house that could be properly opened and closed.
Ontario lumber.
No, Quebec results and Liberal policy.

Warped.
63260-22J
The Address-Mr. Johnston
They were a little warped -I mean the houses.
And the policy.

This is not new to the government because they have been fully informed in regard to it. One would think, sir, that having heard about these things the government would have at least sent out a competent and responsible inspector to see if the statements were correct, and immediately stopped any such practices. But this was not done.
It has been admitted by the government that under the national housing scheme 27,000 houses have been built and under Wartime Housing, 16,000. These houses have been completed and are occupied. As I said last year, I have no great complaint to make about the national housing scheme. I have carefully watched construction from the laying of the foundations to the time the families moved in. I have visited the homes after the families moved in, and I must say that under the national housing scheme the government has done a fairly good job. The material is satisfactory, the workmanship has been well done, and the people are satisfied. But that was done by private contractors, and the individual was allowed free choice of his own contractor. He was permitted to get the design that he required and to go ahead with his house. The government did not assist 'him with any gifts; it was merely a loan which the recipient had to repay at a rate of interest.
Under the two plans the government has built 43,000 houses. We have no indication of how many veterans' houses have been built. At the appropriate time the Minister of Veterans Affairs may tell us how many veterans' houses have been built.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Twenty-sevep hundred.

Last year the department announced that some fifty new homes would be ready for occupancy a few months ago in Calgary. When I left I believe eighteen were occupied. The minister knows that the veterans in Calgary are decidedly -dissatisfied with the conditions of affairs there; he knows it because he has been informed. An organization of veterans was formed in Calgary and the different members of parliament invited to attend meetings. Meetings have been held regularly and I have attended all of them. On different occasions the government inspector has been there. We fiave gone over the problem thoroughly and I am sure that the minister must have been informed by his own representatives of the condition of affairs. If he has not, it is time he removed some of his

officials. May I say that he should start in with some of the inspectors, as I shall indicate as I go along
These houses are costing the veterans a considerable amount of money. When you compare their cost with the cost of the national housing scheme there is not a great deal of difference. I have one house particularly in mind which cost a veteran $5,400, and also a national housing house, just a few blocks away, which cost $6,000. The basement alone of the national housing house is worth the whole of the veteran's house. The veteran's house is going to fall apart in six months. If a good windstorm comes up it will not be there at all; it will look as if an atomic bomb hit it. Five thousand dollars odd is a large sum of money for the type of house the veteran is getting. The houses are valued at too high a figure. The sum of $4,000 is the maximum that should have been paid by the veteran for the house to which I have referred. I can point to dozens of houses that have been privately built in Calgary under the same conditions-better houses by far, and they have not cost $5,400. But I shall refer to that a little later.
To-day I want to take the members of the house and the minister on a visit to these veterans' homes. I am going to confine my visit to Calgary, because I know it is typical of all veterans' houses throughout Canada; I cannot see why it would be different. First of all, let us look at the basements of these veterans' houses. As I said at the beginning, I have watched these houses from the time the basement was dug until the families moved in. Some of the veterans have been in them for three mofiths. I want to be fair; there may be an explanation for this, but out of the eighteen houses that are occupied by veterans in Calgary there may be one or two in which the cement floors and walls have not cracked; in every other case the walls and floors are cracking. The federal government inspector who should inspect these buildings told me that they had put in five bags of cement to the yard in the walls and six bags of cement in the floor. It was a four inch floor. I wish fo address these remarks to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker. Either the inspector is lying or the veterans have taken a bad trimming in the amount of cement that was put into the walls, because no cement wall eight inches thick and no cement floor four inches thick that has - five or six bags of cement to the yard, and the proper proportions of sand and gravel, would ever crack in the manner in which these walls and floors have cracked. The walls and floors are the very foundation upon which the whole house

The Address-Mr. Johnston
is being built. I know enough about cement work to know that there is some funny work somewhere. I say to the minister, through you, sir, that somebody is doing some dirty work somewhere, and when this dirty work is passed on to these veterans it is about time something was done about it.
Let us start with the cement floor. Remember, all these buildings have been inspected and accepted by the federal government inspector. Where his eyes were when he did that, I do not know; they were not in his head. As to the plumbing in the basement, one can go along and take hold of a water pipe and shake it all over. The pipes were not even fastened properly to the joists in the building. In many cases they were leaking. Instead of using galvanized pipe, as I presume the specifications called for, in connecting up the hot water tank, they used ordinary gas pipe. I have not seen the specifications; that may be permissible, but I doubt it very much.
The drain in the basement floor was an inch to an inch and a half above the cement. That meant that when the wife went to do the washing, and drained the washing machine, a great puddle of water lay on the floor which could not be drained out. Had the inspector been there and been doing the job for which he was paid-and paid well, I suppose-he would have tripped over the thing'and probably wakened himself up. I do not think he was ever there; he could not have been, to permit such a thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would my hon. friend be kind enough to tell me exactly where this house is?
Yes; I will do that later.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to know, because I want to follow it up.

Yes, I will do that.
I mentioned to the government last year the material which was going into the veterans' houses. We are still in the basement of this house. I pointed out to the minister that 2 by 8 spruce- joists were used, and that they would not hold up under conditions "as we have them in the west. Nor will they hold up under conditions as you have them in the east. Right over in Hull you have had evidence of that, when houses, built practically of the same material, went to pieces. I pointed this out to the government, but nothing was done.
A beam runs across through the basement to carry the middle weight of the house. When the .joists are laid they are supposed to be long enough to double over the beam; everybody knows that. But in some of these houses the joists do not even reach the beam;
they are spliced in, and the weight comes entirely on the nails. You cannot expect a house so constructed to stand, and it will not stand. As I pointed out to the minister last year, the spruce joists fastened together with one or two spikes where they come across on the beam are coming apart. The result is that the floor above is sagging; it could not be otherwise. The bridgings down in the basement holding the joists were 1 by 2 strips of spruce nailed with 2-inch nails. I told the government that they would not hold up, that as soon as these narrow strips dried out you could pull the nails out with your fingers; and that is exactly what is happening. There is hardly one of these small bridgings which you cannot pull off with one or two fingers; the joists are twisted, and the house is going to be twisted as well. If this happens after they have been occupied for only two or three months, what is going to happen when the heat strikes them at 110 degrees in the shade?
Have these houses passed inspection?

Yes, they have all been passed by the government inspector. I shall refer to that government inspector a little later.
I have not seen the specifications of these houses. I think there are different specifications for each house. But the city by-law definitely prohibits the use of anything less than a 2 by 2 for bridging, yet the government has put in 1 by 2 spruce.
Let me now take you up to the first floor of one of these houses. Incidentally, in walking up to the first floor one of the men fell through the stairs. He did not trip, either. I should like to give the minister a picture of these houses that our veterans have to live in; and may I tell him that their wives are not very well satisfied when for twenty-four hours a day they have to live in these places. Imagine a wife who is doing her washing and drains the washing machine and finds the basement floor filled with water, which will not run off. It is not a very pleasant situation to be in.
We are now on the first floor, the main floor. As hon. members know, these walls are 4 by 8 sheets of plaster board. Plaster board is something like gyproc lap, but in larger sheets, and if you use small headed nails in putting on the plaster boards they will not hold. Some of these nails have small heads, others have larger heads, but the type of head used was the small-headed nail, the very poorest one which could be chosen, with the result that the boards are loose on the.

The Address-Mr. Johnston
walls and in a great many cases have to be gone over and renailed. I never, Mr. Speaker, saw such a miserably poor job of workmanship. It is possible to have a nicely finished room by using plaster "board, and I have seen houses in which it has been used, where the joints have been properly cemented before the tape was put over, and sanded down, and after painting the joint is completely invisible. But in these houses you could look clear across the place and see the joint as clearly as you could see the wall, right through the paint. All across the ceiling you can see these joints running clear across. Imagine the wife of a veteran who is entertaining her friends in the evening, with these big strips of tape running across the wall. One finds that throughout the house. It is faulty workmanship, not faulty material in this case. The joists in the basement were faulty material, and the government was responsible for them; what I am speaking of now is a matter of faulty workmanship. But the government is responsible, because it should know the contractor to whom it let the contracts for these buildings, and the inspector who passed them.
Where the walls come to the corner it is usual in all well-built houses to have a metal bead running down the corner. In these houses instead of having metal bead they have a 2 by 2 spruce on the edges of the partition. The 2 by 2-1 am speaking now generally of the finish-was never sanded off when it was painted; it was furry before it was put up, and when it is painted in that condition you cannot remedy it without sandpapering all the paint off. There was no attempt to finish up the cheap material used in the comers .in this building instead of metal beads.
The doors are not properly hung. Hardly a door is properly hung. On one occasion when they came to repair these buildings they put pasteboard behind the hinges to even things up around the door, but the gap is still there. It was faulty1 workmanship, but still the inspector passed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Is this the same
house?

No. I have visited
several.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How many?
I would say I have visited half a dozen of the eighteen, but those who were at these meetings told me that conditions were almost the same in all these houses.
I think you would make a good inspector.

I could do better than that; there is no question about it. Even the hon. member himself could, I think. He has a fine house, I understand.
Now let us go to the flooring. The floor was supposed to be No. 1 edge grain flooring. Edge grain flooring has no knots in it. This is not No. 1 edge grain fir flooring, yet the veteran is paying for it. I remember one house in particular when the inspector was present and the man who owned this house was complaining about the knots in the floor right in the front part of the room. He said he did not know how that could be; and one of the other fellows said, "Well, if you recall, when you inspected the house it was covered with paper." I said to the inspector, "Did you not raise this paper when you went in to inspect the building for the government?"- and he said he had not. How can a government inspector go through a house and inspect floors that are covered with paper-even looking at them? That is something no woman wants in her front room-knots all over the floor. The veteran was paying for No. 1 material, but he did not get it.
Let us go upstairs-but be careful of your head, because you will have it bumped. That is the government's fault, the architect's fault. I am not a tall man, but I know the minister would have to get- down on his knees to go up there.
It would do him no harm.

No, it would not. He should get down and pray for these poor veterans who have got such a fleecing. Now, that is the architect's fault. I do not blame the contractor for it, because I imagine it was that way in his specifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Who was the contractor? I do not know where the house was.
If you want me to name it-Bennett and White.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where is the house?
In Calgary.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Calgary is a big place.

It is a fine place; you ought to come out there. Now, that was the main staircase going upstairs. One has to duck his dead as he goes up. That is not a very satisfactory state of affairs, 'as the minister will no doubt agree. However, I shall not prolong this phase of the matter.

The Address-Mr. Johnston
I want to say something about windows. Here I am not blaming the contractor so much as I am the government. When the windows were put into these houses they were fitted for sash cords and weights, and ploughed out for that purpose. But when those windows were installed, no sash cords or weights were put in, nor was there provision made for it. The windows were already ploughed, and as a result when the wind blows it goes right up both sides of the window and simply blows out the curtains. As anyone knows, with the wind blowing in like that, and blowing the curtains, it is not a very satisfactory state of affairs.
I am skipping over quite a bit of the detail, because my time is limited. I do wish to speak about heating. It will be understood that as I go along I am picking out the major items. If I were to deal with all the minor items it would take a very long time.
The heating is a gravity system. When it comes to the first floor, the registers are in the wall. That is the proper place for them. But the cold air vents are on the floor, and they are placed out about ten inches from the wall. They are oblong in shape, about ten inches wide and about sixteen inches long, fitting in between the joists. There are wooden slats across them, and those slats are about one-quarter inch by li inches, and sixteen inches long. There they are, sitting I was about to say, almost in the middle of the floor, ten inches from the wall; and if a person came in there and put his chair in that part of the room it would go right down through the floor. Besides, it is a regular dirt trap. One cannot put chairs in the vicinity, because someone would fall through it-a very unsatisfactory condition. The wooden grills should have been put in the wall.
When one goes upstairs he finds that the hot-air vents are placed in the floors. These are just metal grates, not fastened down in any way. All the dirt falls down into them. The children could very easily throw articles in there-in fact they could even get in themselves. The hot-air vents should have been in the wall. It would have cost practically no more to put them in the proper place than to stick them out in the middle of the room, as they are now. These are conditions which should be rectified.
I did a little estimating on this house, which cost $5,400, and I do not think I am far out. I have estimated the plumbing at $400.
How many rooms?

Five or six; I am not just sure which. An ordinary plumbing job for such a house would cost about $475, but I
think the government would get it for a little less than that, and for that reason I cut it down to $400. The city works section would cost about $400, and the lumber about $1,600.
I have made that figure a maximum, because I do not think it should cost more than that for the type of house in question. That would make a total of $2,400, and to this should be added the carpentry work as the remaining cost item, approximately $3,000 for the carpentry work on those houses. I say a contractor has no right to receive $3,000 for building a house of that kind. It is entirely too much money; $2,000 would be enough. And for that he should do a good job.
Someone will say, "Oh, well; they have to pay high wages." They are not paying high wages. When it comes to the matter of having skilled workers to build a house, I say one does not have to have all skilled workers. All one needs to build a house, and to build it properly, is to have one or two good carpenters. The rest can be nail drivers. In this way one can build a first-class house, in first-class condition. There is no scarcity of labour in that regard.
Had the house a basement?

Yes, this house had a basement. Another complaint I have is that these contractors are getting approximately $3,000 for the carpenter work, and the government supplies the material; then they sublet contracts for laying floors, putting on lath, etc.
When I refer to floors there is something further I should add. I have been skipping along so fast that I have been leaving out important details. In laying the upstairs floors they laid the spruce lumber groove to groove and tongue to tongue-and that was passed by a government inspector. In the kitchen they put down first-class battleship linoleum over the spruce floors. Of course the spruce shrunk, and the linoleum drew in, with the result that there is a quarter of an inch space down the middle of the kitchen. Adjustments have had to be made in these things. In fact they sent a carpenter up there at extra expense to the government, because the contractor got extra for this.
Was the inspector one of those dollar-a-year men, or how was he paid for inspecting?
The hon. member will have to ask the minister that question. I do not think he is working for a dollar a year. I think he is a Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that?

It sounds like it.
The Address-Mr. Johnston

I think it is a wrong
practice to permit the contractor to sublet his contracts for laying floors, putting on plaster board, or putting on this or that. He sublets for shingling, for flooring, and for this or that.
This procedure of building veterans' houses or war-time houses on a mass production basis is wrong. We give a contract for 300 or 400 houses to one man, and then he starts to build the houses on' a mass scale, subletting this and subletting that. Why not let them out to private contractors who will do the job under proper and decent conditions? Why should not a man have some say about the house he is to live in, or have some supervision over its construction, especially when he has to pay for it? Surely he should have something to say about it.
What are we going to do to rectify these unsatisfactory conditions? My estimate is-* and I do not think I am far wrong-that it will cost from $500 to $1,000 more to condition these houses so that they will be at all passable, and so that veterans can live in them.
1 believe, as I have said, that it will cost the government from $500 to $1,000 more to put these houses into such condition that they can be lived in. And even when that much has been spent, still we shall not have proper houses, because as soon as the heat strikes in the summer the damage will continue. The men who have bought these houses should be permitted to have new ones. I do not think they should be asked to live in these places. The government should immediately stop building houses with spruce. Of course they contend that there is a shortage of material, but I would rather have one good house built than two poor ones, and I would rather have one veteran satisfied with his home than have two dissatisfied. I do not think we would be so short of material if we stopped shipping out the best of our materials to other countries. Let us keep some here to build houses for these men whom just a few short months ago we were calling great heroes-, whom just a few short months ago we were meeting with bands, for whom just a few short months ago we had signs up in the stations, "Welcome home, boys." Then we give them one of these houses. That is not good enough.
The government should do everything possible to remedy these conditions, and I am sure the minister will, now that the matter has been brought to his attention. Proper precautions should be taken. These veterans should not be told, and I know they would not be told by the minister, what was told

to the chairman of this committee by a government representative: The chairman of this committee was told, "You can either take it or get out." I said to them, "Don't be afraid of his kicking you out, because I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs will not stand for anything like that." Maybe I was speaking out of turn, but I do not think so.
That is not the way to talk to these men. All they want is satisfaction. They want something for the money they are paying, because they feel that they have earned their gratuities. They feel that they have some right to fair treatment. I hope the minister will take this matter under advisement and have an immediate check made of these things. Efforts should be made to see that these men are satisfied and that they have houses to which their wives and families will not be ashamed to bring their friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In order to carry out the request made by my hon. friend, will he kindly tell me the exact location of the house in question?
I have not the exact address, but I will give it to the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What did the veteran pay for the house?
That is plenty.

These conditions are not applicable to just one house. I know of another man, and I am not going to tell you his politics although I think the minister would be pleased if I did. Before this man felt he could move in he spent over S250 out of his own pocket to finish the house. He did a fairly good job, but they dare not put a piano in the house because the floor now looks like a camel's back.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that the same house?
No, it is a different one.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In the same location?
Yes, it is the same location, up on North Hill, where veterans' houses are being built in Calgary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. member sure that those houses were built under the land act administration?

Oh, yes. Mr. Finlater is one of the inspectors and Mr. Turner is the other. Bennett and White were the contractors.

The Address-Mr. Bryce
That is the small holdings development?
That is right, out at North Hill.

Mr. Speaker, I have refrained from taking part in this debate because I was one of the lesser lights who went to the continent this year and I was waiting until the greater lights had had their say. I was greatly taken with what I saw there. I was interested in what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had to say the other day. He finished his remarks with these words, which will be found on page 97 of Hansard:
One found a condition there which gave one a certain impression. I came away from Paris feeling that I had seen a very dejected people, a people who were suffering because of need, a people who were not properly clothed, a people who required a great deal of sympathy >and care from those of us outside.
I had intended to demonstrate the benefits I had derived from my visit to France by speaking in French, but there are so few of my French-speaking friends here this afternoon that I am just going to stick to my own doric. No person can understand or realize what the French people have gone through. Perhaps those members on both sides of the house who' fought over the Normandy beaches, up through Falaise, Caen, Amiens and right on through know what it is like because they were through the worst of it. We must remember that when we were not in France, the Germans were. These people were bombed incessantly. If the Germans were not bombing them, we were. This put us in a rather awkward position. We would meet people who had lost legs and arms and naturally we would say, "How did you lose your leg?" or "How did you lose your arm?" A man might reply, "Well, one of your airmen came over one night."
I want hon. members to realize that these people have suffered as no other nation has suffered. England and Scotland also suffered, but they are taking it right on the chin. Hon. members have no idea of how they are taking it. I went to my native city and they said, "We were not damaged at all," but in two nights Jerry destroyed 4,500 homes. Still they said they were not damaged. Then we hear members in this House of Commons say that [DOT] we should not lend them money to help them get back on their feet or reinstate themselves. Those hon. members just do not understand because they have not had an opportunity to see like the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler), the hon. member for Winnipeg
North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and other hon. members. We saw the terrible conditions
that exist.
In Paris I saw people line up at seven o'clock in the morning to try to get food. This was not in front of the Ritz either. I stayed at the Ritz to see what it was like.
Where did you get all the money?

I travelled with a Conservative. I saw those poor people standing in line waiting with their coupons for bread. They would wait until ten or half-past ten o'clock and then they would be told, "No bread to-day." We neker had anything like that. The nearest they got to us was the St. Lawrence river. We should be ready to go down on our knees and thank these people for what they saved us from. Our boys and girls went there and did their part, but we folk at home never knew what was going on.
When you speak to the British people they will tell you that they have plenty of food, that they never wanted' for anything at all. I have in my hand a book entitled, "Dainty Dishes for ths Queen." This contains 160 recipes for dishes made out of oatmeal and potatoes.
That is good Scotch food.

I know we have big men like the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) who have been raised on meal and potatoes, but believe me that gets pretty monotonous, and that is what is going on in the old country to-day. I make this plea to everyone who has friends in the old country: Send them a parcel, for they will appreciate it. I had the pleasure, with other members of this house, of seeing people over there receive parcels from Canada, and they were just like kids around a Christmas tree. They were so pleased to get something different from what they usually had. We were in places in France where, when we .got up in the morning, we could get no breakfast and had to drive to the next town before we could get anything to eat. That is a deplorable state of affairs. When we did get a good meal and asked how that came about, the answer was that the food was procured in the black market.
France is up against a problem which no other country in the world faces to-day. For the last five or six years French boys in their teens, from fifteen up to twenty, have been trained in the underground movement to believe that they were heroes if they killed a German or disrupted the then government service. Now they have a government of their own, but they do not yet icalize that it is
33S
The Address-Mr. Bryce
Coming through the rye.

The argument put up by these gentlemen who speculate in futures is the future market. I have the figures here, showing that on December 7, 1945, there were visible in Canada 1,442,000 bushels, and on February 1, 1946, there were 1,458,000 bushels, or 16,000 bushels more on the futures market. We are told that when there is less the price should go up and when there is more the price should go down. But here the price jumped from 81.81^ to S2.29L This Liberal government sends representatives to a food conference with the idea of feeding the world, and it will pay a farmer ninety cents or $1 for his rye and then allow these fellows to gamble in the commodity, while the poor man who has to turn it into bread pays 82.60 a bushel for it. One wonders how people can do such things. If it is good for wheat, oats and barley to be under the control of the wheat board, then the same arguments apply to rye.
I do not know whether I have made that argument strong enough, but I feel that this is one of the greatest injustices the government has done to the common man, because the man who produces rye produces it in the poorest ground. Up in the interlake country where there is nothing but sand they will grow rye, and some of the most underpaid people in the world eat rye bread to-day; yet the government will allow these privileged few to gamble in the produce of the farmer. There is no place in the modern world for gambling in food.
I have some other things I wish to discuss but perhaps I have said enough for the present. However, I will say this to the government. We need live stock legislation to protect the farmer, just as we need a wheat board. You can call it anything you like. I am not fussy about the name. When I made the proposal before, I called it a board of live stock commissioners, and it was suggested that it might not be legal. Well, the members of this government have enough brains to get over such technicalities, if they want to use those brains. I hope they will use them and give us a live stock marketing board to protect the farmer, because he will need that protection.
There have been great changes over the last thirty years. We no longer market our produce in a haphazard way. If you want quality and you establish grades, then I submit that the farmers should be given some say
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

in the fixing of those grades. It is absolutely necessary that they should have representation on any board. I am not suggesting that the, packer is not also entitled to representation on it, as well as the consumer and all others concerned. But let everyone be represented on the board.

In the first place I congratulate the two hon. members who have just spoken; and I will remind the latter that the late King George once admonished the Prince of Wales because he had been speculating in grain. The teachings of the king were to the same effect as the speech of my hon. friend, that there should be no speculation in grain and especially in rye because it is a kind of grain that is just as good to drink as to eat.
We need some reform in this country; we need reform in a. broad spirit; but all those who desire to obtain reform must realize in advance that they will get no place, to use slang language, unless they have the determination to suffer slander, insult and abuse for the good cause. That was my experience. Yesterday I received a clipping of a dirty sheet that is published at noontime in Montreal. I shall read it in a moment, but before I read it I shall make a correction in Hansard. At page 220 I am reported as having said, speaking of Colonel Bovey:
The mai) who makes molasses peaches . . .
I never said that. I did not say that he had received pay as one of the 140 who make preserved peaches, but I said that he was making molasses speeches, sticky speeches for his own benefit. That is what I said and afterwards I complained of McGill university being a red house. By the same mail I received a clipping from the Gazette of March 19 with the picture of Tim Buck addressing the students of McGill, and the gentleman wrote me a very fine letter which I will send to my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) who stated a few truths that were denied by Principal James.
By the same mail I received an editorial of that dirty sheet. I shall read one paragraph. I have some other excerpts from newspapers which I shall read later on:
Montreal, Wednesday, March 27, 1946.
Something has been added' to the "hotbed of communism" charges levelled at McGill by -Solon Low-endorsation from the lips of J. F. Pouliot, M.P.
Most- Canadians are familiar with Mr. Pouliot's near perfect record for inaugurating and supporting groundless accusations, designed to increase disunity and embarrass governments and institutions.
Only that; that is all I have to say about that remark. I will not say it is inspired 
by anyone, but I prescribe a triple dose of castor oil to the writer of this editorial and a similar one to Colonel Bovey. That is my. potion.
I shall draw the attention of the members of the house to the fact that one thing has been said for the public good by the leader of the Social Credit group and I have repeated it in asking for. some reform. Instead of securing any reform, we get abuse from a paper which is inspired by the very man. of whom we complain, because they give the wrong information to us; that is all. My hon. friend was the victim of some abuse and so was I. I am far from suffering from the mania of persecution; but I wish to point out that nothing will be accomplished unless all members of parliament have the triple armour of steel around their breasts to defy all the iniquitous persons whom we may meet on the way to reform.
That is my first point, and I have other incidents. There is a young man who lived for a time in the Saguenay district, lake St. John. He was the public relations officer of a big company. He gave false news and led the cabinet and a minister into error. That man never corrected himself. He is now in the eastern townships in charge of a paper. When I received very great honour he wrote this article which appeared in the Sherbrooke Record of February 4, 1946:
In many quarters Mr. Pouliot is regarded as rather irresponsible and as something of a firebrand.
Afterwards he said that apparently it was right, but there was some insult and innuendo in his article. It was the old story, that one cannot complain of any parasite, profiteer, pirate, highway robber or thief without having bad motives. One must have bad motives, no manners at all. What has happened? Of course, I never belonged to the army, but I was described in my constituency last December as a friend of the draftees and the soldiers alike, friend of both. They gave me a dinner and presented me with a brand new car, which is something that is appreciated, because it is the only county where it has been done. It has been done for my provincial mate. Before that, it was done only for one other member of parliament, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who had a big square automobile in the old days. It is something that touched me very deeply.
It would touch anybody.

Yes. I hope that the constituents of my hon. friend give him the finest limousine because he deserves it.

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
I come now to the Victoria Cross. I am interested in the recipients of this medal and when I spoke about the McGill students I mentioned that. Your Honour did something for one of the winners which is merited, but it is not enough. However, Your Honour did more for him than anyone else had done. The press took it up and! it was reported in the papers of Victoria. I received word from another hero in British Columbia who had received the Victoria Cross from the hands of our king during the first war. By the way, he was the first officer of the Canadian army to receive the Victoria Cross, and he passed above the heads of everybody in British Columbia, above the heads of all members of parliament, even those who had a very fine war record, even above the head of the legion, to send an S.O.S. to Jean Francois Pouliot in lower Quebec. I consider it a very great honour and, to be just and fair, I will say that the minister is doing his best to fix up this case, with the assistance of his most valuable parliamentary assistant. It is something which touches one, that a hero of the last war, who has been abandoned by all, goes far away, thousands of miles from his district, to get in touch with one who is ready to fight for him. I took up his case, and at the same time that the newspapers said that apparently it was worthy of consideration, they said of me, "In many quarters Mr. Pouliot is regarded as rather irresponsible and as something of a firebrand." Those who are afraid to be called names by such a nonentity will obtain no reform; and I tell my colleagues, for whom I have great respect, that if they want any reform in this country they have only one thing to do, namely, not to be afraid to say what they believe is right and what they believe is for a good purpose.
There is something else; and I come to the crucial point. Last year hon. gentlemen who listened to me will remember how difficult it was to unearth the amount of money which was earned by the firm of Borden and Company in Toronto. How many times did I rise in the house to ask for that information? I was told that everything that was earned by the firm was returned to the government in a mood of sacrifice and generosity on the altar of the country.
You believed that, of course ?

I did not believe it at all, and (that is why I asked the question. I asked for copies of the cheques which had been sent for the amounts of moneys received. It was no insult; it was a matter of fact, that the man who- was there in the department was looking after his own interests. What did the Globe and Mail say about the member for Temiscouata? I cannot complain very much about the Globe and Mail; I have much more respect for it than for the Sherbrooke Record and for the other dirty sheet which is published in Montreal. I have had great respect for the Globe and Mail since the days of Harry Anderson, who was a dear friend of mine.
He was a very fine man.

Certainly. My hon. friend knows I had the honour of being amongst Mr. Anderson's friends; and when his picture was unveiled for the press gallery I was one of the very few members who, along with the then Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), were invited there. I appreciated that very much. I had and I still have very good friends in the province of Ontario. But what I say about the Globe and Mail is what Poujoulat, a great French author, said of Cardinal Richelieu:
Le cardinal m'a fait trop de bien pour que j'en dise d'u mal; le cardinal m'a fait trop de mal pour que j'en dise du bien.
That is, "The cardinal has done too much good to me for me to speak badly of him, and he has done too much evil for me to say anything good about him." But I will say something nevertheless; and I will read what has been written about me in the Toronto Globe and Mail to humiliate me. That was the purpose, but it was not realized, because I have the skin of a crocodile. Nevertheless the purpose was to humiliate me, to abuse me, to treat me with insult, to make me suffer humiliation. Here it is:
A malicious attack.
Imagine; a man who is malicious, a man who wants to do harm to someone! I am astonished that the title was not "a blasphemous attack". It should have been, because down there they still believe in the golden calf. There are some in Toronto, as there are in Montreal and other places.
Mr. Jean Francoi-s Pouliot staged in the House of Commons on Wednesday another of his many deplorable performances -as -a public mischief-maker.
That is inoffensive!

What an abomination!
-Munitions Minister Howe, Hinder whom Mr. Borden served, came to his defence with a categorical denial of Mr. Pouliot's defamatory charges.

Pouliot was right, arid his charges were not defamatory. I did not write to the Globe and Mail. But I put a question before the house, so that the house knows that when Pouliot asks a question, if he does not know all the details he at least has good reason for asking that question, and knows something about it.
I have too much respect for the house, including my colleagues, to make any false statements to it or to them respecting mafc-ters of fact. Of course I may err when 1 express an opinion, but when I state a fact I can always prove it. If someone wants information I will answer, and will tell my source of information, so that the house may know about it in a definite way.
My first conclusion is that one who has not been affected by the atmosphere of Ottawa will not be affected to any considerable extent by the unfair criticism of some of the local newspapers which are controlled by interests which always cater to- bureaucracy. One must make his own judgments. One must not take for granted that everything said to him is true, and that because something is said by Mr. So-and-so it must be right. Therefore I tell my colleagues, whom I respect, that if they want to continue their war against bureaucracy, and- to bring back responsible government in Canada, they are sure to be abused and to be slandered; they are sure to be minimized in the eyes of their electors!
I am not alone in that category. I remember well the insults that were heaped upon us at the time of the sittings of the civil service committee. My hon. friends were on that committee serving with me. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) served- on it, and did excellent work, as did the other members. 'It gives me pleasure to offer them praise for what they did.
That is my first observation. Then I have another point I would ask hon. members to keep in mind. While I have the deepest respect for returned men and while I am . always ready to help them, and want to have the help of the minister and his assistant- because apparently they are two of tjie very few good men in the department-yet we must not lose our sense of proportion. Because a man has done excellent work during the war, it does not necessarily follow that he must be considered infallible in anything he does afterwards, in any field of action.
For instance, it was ridiculous to consider as infallible two former defence ministers, simply because each had a fine war record. It was silly to do that. But I could not contradict either Power or Ralston because both had fine war records. It is'true; I concede it;

The Address-Mr. Wylie
I admit it. But that is no reason why one should not find any fault in the managing of their departments. Those who believed them infallible were simply credulous, and behaving like children. I have too much respect for members of parliament to let them fall into such credulity, which is childish.
I have one thing further to say, and I shall have finished. It is to repeat in another form what I said when I was sitting on the opposite side of the house, at a time when I suggested we should have a union opposition, composed of all liberal-minded members of parliament. That was a time when the clean-up which has been made in the three defence departments had not been completed, and I felt it was time to do something about it.
We are here to do something; we are not here just to make speeches. We are here to reform the government of the dominion, so that we can do something beneficial for the common people. I give credit to all hon. members that they intend to do something for the country. We will do it together, if we remove obstacles to progress.
If we are to deal effectively with bureaucracy, with fairness and with equity, keeping in mind at the same time the usefulness of civil servants to the state-and this is not being done by the commission now making an investigation-and if we want to make a clean-up of the civil service, then we must first of all make a clean-up in all political parties, so that liberal-minded men may act together, whether they be Liberals, Conservatives by name, Social Crediters, or in the C.C.F. group. That is not important.
' We are reaching a time when there will be a great cleavage in Canada between people who are thinking about the future of the country. There will be those who have a Canadian spirit and who think of Canada before any other country; and on the other side there will be those who think of any other country before Canada. Let us put them under the same roof and in the same corner.
What shall we do? In the first place the two old parties shall get rid of the control of international finance. I have mentioned something about Mr. Borden. He may be a good lawyer, and I have not attacked his reputation as such. I said, too, that he had collected funds for his party-perhaps for both major parties- when he was working as controller. I find nothing scandalous in that. People become scandalized over things which ought not to affect them in that way.
But he is now the adviser to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). He is the man who was with Ralston, and who belongs to the DunningrRalston group in Montreal, the international finance promoters and agents. He is not the kind of man who khould be adviser to the leader of a great political party-and just on account of that fact.
He was controller of controllers here in Ottawa, a position he should never have had, but he did have it, because of the influence of Ralston, who was sitting with him at Barclay's.
Who is the chairman of the National Liberal Federation? It is Gordon Fogo, a former law partner of Ralston, who was assistant to Borden in the Department of Munitions and Supply, holding the position of acting controller of controllers. I want to get rid of them. I want to clean out the party of all these rascals and pirates. I want the Canadian people to know where we are. The party should have a definite policy. If our policy is to be a Canadian policy, let it be a Canadian policy throughout Canada. If it is to be an imperialistic policy, let us make it an imperialistic policy also in Quebec, so that the people of Quebec will not be deceived when the election comes around. That is enough for to-day, but it will be continued at some other time.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate at this late date I find myself in the same position as many hon. members who have spoken during the past two days. I had not intended to take part in this debate, but since our rules were more or less broken on Tuesday I decided that I might just as well get into the debate with the rest of the speakers from the different parties.
No reference was made in the speech from the throne to several matters of paramount importance to Canada, and in particular to western Canada. We have listened to many important speeches during this debate and have heard many important issues discussed, but I wish to touch upon two matters which, in my opinion, are most important to the people of my riding, to southern Alberta and to Canada as a whole. It is not that I think the other matters are not important; I certainly think they are important and I may take an opportunity of discussing them at some later date in the session.
I am confining my remarks mainly to two issues, irrigation and the trans-Canada highway. Those issues affect the future development, prosperity and economic welfare of southern Alberta in particular and of Canada as a whole. I wish to take this opportunity to thank the hon. member for Dav.enport (Mr. MacNicol) for the interest he has taken in the irrigation of western Canada and in particular for the meeting which he held in
The Address-Mr. Wylie

Medicine Hat in, January. My only regret is that I was unable to be at that meeting. I was in the hospital at the time, but from all reports I have heard that meeting was certainly one of the best meetings they ever held in Medicine Hat. There is no one better qualified to discuss irrigation than the hon. member for Davenport. I am sure he knows every coulee and where every dam should be put in connection with either the St. Mary's-Milk river project or the Redcliff-Ronalane project.
The residents of the drought area are fully aware of the fact that irrigation is the only solution of our crop-failure-due-to-drought problems, and that is the reason why more extensive efforts to obtain irrigation have been made during the past year than ever before. It might be well to enumerate for the information of the house some of the support which has been given to this effort during the past year. I shall mention only a few of the organizations that have supported this matter, but I believe they should be mentioned. These are:

Alberta Board of Trade and Agriculture
Medicine Hat City Council
Medicine Hat Branch of the Canadian Legion
Medicine Hat Chamber of Commerce
Medicine Tat Trades and Labour Council
Redcliff public meeting
