Various clubs in Medicine Hat as well as other organizations and individuals have given their support to these irrigation projects. I should like to read one paragraph frqm a resolution which was passed by the Medicine Hat trades and labour council, because this will give the house an idea of just how the residents of that area are looking at this project. They said:
We have given billions to Britain and other European countries, 750 million to the Export Credit Act, 750 million td Bretton Woods. Increased the capital of the T.-C.A. from 5 million to 25 million. Now surely we can give to our own -people enough to give them the horn of plenty, that they deserve.
I wish to state right away that the Medicine Hat trades and labour council do not object to the money we have given to the people of Britain. Those people have given much more than we in this country have given, as the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) has just said in his most interesting speech. Simply because it is mentioned in their resolution does not mean that they are opposed to the idea. They believe that when we can do that for other countries there is no reason why we cannot do something for our 	.
own people. That is why they say that in their resolution. Irrigation is the formula for an all-out Canadian prosperity. The east is dependent upon the west for its prosperity. It is in the interests of the dominion as a whole to place the prairies on a sound financial footing.
The projects most urgently needed could be undertaken first. As other areas are brought into greater and more suitable productiveness, the drain upon the government for drought relief would be lessened. The gains at first may be small, but as the areas under the ditch are increased the field of prosperity will be steadily enlarged and the need for assistance correspondingly lowered.
The St. Mary's-Milk river and Redeliff-Ronalave projects, can be described as an urgent need owing to deficient rainfall in that area and the feasibility of both projects. The provision of work when needed is important but this should not be the primary objective. The main purpose of water conservation and irrigation in southern Alberta is to rehabilitate the farming industry in that area. That is why such strong protests were made when it was suggested that both projects be placed in the category of an employment stop-gap. It is true, however, that the construction of irrigation works provides jobs, which is an added reason for the early completion of both projects, in view of the prevailing unemployment situation.
Mr. Speaker, the year 1945, like so many in the past, was another drought year. The devastating effects were extensive and far-reaching. This, following two years of drought, which were almost as serious, brings severe hardships to many farmers, and hundreds of farmers find themselves in the same position as they were in, in 1937, in having to dispose of their cattle herds. While stock prices were good, the majority of cattle were sold as feeders, which of course meant a loss to the farmers. Many cattle in that area have died this winter on account of the feed shortage. Feed was hard to get and had to be hauled long distances, mainly from the irrigation districts of Brooks and the Taber-Lethbridge area. The development of the projects mentioned would change this situation materially. The placing of the available watqr on these lands is the finest type of crop insurance against drought. For a long time we in the south have known that we have the natural garden climate of western Canada. This area can be made into one of the great producing areas of this continent. All that is required is to make water available when and where it is needed. Experience has proven

The Address-Mr. Wylie
that we cannot depend upon natural rainfall to provide sufficient moisture for the growing crops. There is, however, sufficient water running to useless and inexcusable waste down the South Saskatchewan river to irrigate almost a million acres of the best land in Alberta, and still have plenty of water for various projects in Saskatchewan, also water for Moose Jaw, which the hon. member for that city mentioned in his able speech last week.
With reference to the St. Mary's-Milk river project, international waters are involved and Canada has long neglected to make beneficial use of its share, while the United States of America has built reservoir facilities to store practically the whole flow. Unless we make a more combined effort to use our rightful share, the United States might claim this on the basis of prior use. We must remember that every drop of water which runs to the sea without rendering a commercial return is a public waste.
I have an illustrated pamphlet prepared by the eastern irrigation district at Brooks, of which E. W. Brunsden is general manager. I am sure most hon. members received this pamphlet. It is interesting and shows what can be accomplished by turning water on the soil.
On the first page it shows a lovely field of sugar beets and says, "This proven irrigation project has everything a food processor seeks." Then it shows part of the irrigation works, the Bassano dam, also the Brooks aqueduct, with two miles of continuous concrete conduit. It also shows the flume at Lathom, a fifteen-foot semi-circular wood stave, half a mile long, and various other pictures of interest. It gives the hours of sunshine. I do not think it is necessary for me to describe the pamphlet in detail because I am sure most hon. members have received a copy. It is a well known fact, of course, that under our present system of dry land farming out there we get too much sunshine and not enough rainfall. It also shows the long frost-free period, which of course is beneficial to irrigation. The southern part of the province has the longest frost-free period in the west, due no doubt to the Chinooks that we get in that part. The productivity of the soil in that area is also shown, not only in the Brooks area but in the south. It also tells about the specialized crops that may be produced to get away from wheat farming. It says this about specialized crops:
The farmers of the eastern irrigation district are not one-crop farmers. They long have practised diversification. Potatoes, 'alfalfa and sweet clover for hay and seed; sugar beets, radish, beetroot, mustard and peas for seed are
among the crops successfully grown over periods of years in addition to .all of the -cereal and coarse grains and flax.
It also mentions the high quality of the live stock of all types produced in that district. This is a natural result in an irrigation district where there is an abundance of feed.

Before the house rises may I ask the hon. member to write to the publisher of the pamphlet to which he has just referred and ask that a copy be sent to each member of the house. I did not get a copy, and the hon. member to my left and the hon. member in front of me did not receive a copy. It would do no harm and might do a lot of good.

Mr. Speaker, before the
dinner recess I was dealing with an illustrated pamphlet showing what can be grown in the district of southern Alberta under irrigation. There are a few more points in this pamphlet which I wish to touch upon, such as types of food processing plants. For example, they have vegetable canning, and I understand they are getting a new factory this year which will mean a great deal to that district. There are small fruit canning and quick-freeze plants, to which farmers can take their fruit, have it quickly frozen and take it out as they wish, using it as fresh fruit.- There are also pickle packing establishments for cucumbers, cauliflower, onions and so on, and there are also meat processing plants. They have not a sugar beet factory at the present time but have high hopes of securing one in the near future. There is a move on now whereby, by next fall, they expect to have a plant.
The farmers of that area are so convinced of this that they went out and raised $600,000 in a matter of a few days to assist in building this factory, and they hope that the same results will not befall this undertaking that happened to the last factory which they planned on building.
There are also dairy products and poultry packing plants. That all goes with irrigation. Them, last but not least, this pamphlet shows the wonderful homes of the farmers in that area. There are twelve hundred farm families at present in- the area and their homes would be a credit to any district. In my travels around this part of Canada I have found very few homes that compare with those in the irrigation district. By that I do not mean that the homes in the west are as large as
The Address-Mr. Wylie

they are here. They are more of the cottage type. But they are all painted and' have lovely lawns, with beautiful shrubs surrounding the farms, so that they are a credit to the district.
The last page shows a picture of the Bassano dam, which would be of interest to many members of the house. I am sorry that all members have not received that pamphlet. I was under the impression that they had all received it until the contrary was called to my attention by the hoa. member for Davenport.
In "Alberta's eastern irrigation" district, where water works wonders," the charge for water is approximately $1.60 to $1.75 per irrigable acre, so that the cost is not so high considering what the farmers produce.
The pamphlet goes on to show what is raised on the irrigated land, giving the number of bushels per acre and other information. I hope that more of these pamphlets will be circulated in the near future.
Going from the irrigation district to the drought area, which comprises most of my riding, you run into an entirely different situation. You pass into an area where during the last three years the average yield of wheat has been less than four bushels to the acre. The Minister of Agriculture can very easily verify this by reference to the amounts paid to the farmers through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Not only that; there are farmers who have stock that is in poor shape for the reason that no feed has been grown. The homes are not so good-that is, the majority of the homes-as in the irrigation district. They lack trees around the buildings and also windbreaks, and that would mean a great deal in southern Alberta as well as in southern Saskatchewan, where we have plenty of Chinook winds. It would tend to break the wind not only in the summer but also in the winter.
In passing, I wish to make a few remarks regarding the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That act has helped, of course, the majority of the farmers in this area. If it had not been for the act they would have found themselves very much the same as in 1937, back on relief, not only as regards direct relief but in the matter of agricultural advances as well. However, many changes are necessary in the act, and I hope we shall have an opportunity, before the session ends, to discuss some of the important revisions that should be made.
The question of farm products prices has been dealt with thoroughly by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and I do not think it is necessary for me to go over that again. The prosperity of Medicine Hat

depends entirely on this irrigation system. There are many businesses waiting until the irrigation system is developed and, after all, we cannot blame the businessmen, because we have had promises of irrigation for twenty-five or thirty years and not very much has been done.
I was talking to a garage man the other day and he was interested in irrigation projects. He said to me, "If I were sure of irrigation being developed in this area I would increase my establishment; I would build a garage twice this size." That is only one example of conditions in Medicine Hat at the present time. During the war we had No. 34 S.F.T.S. and the prisoner of war camp also brought many residents into the city so that conditions were improved somewhat. Now, however, these are both being closed. As a matter of fact, 'one has been closed and the closing of the other will soon follow. When that happens Medicine Hat will revert to what it was before the war.
We hope thaf what the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) mentioned is correct, that we can expect a fifty per cent reduction in our taxes this year. We shall wait and see with interest. I agree with the leader of this party who, in his able speech, suggested that the personal income tax schedule should be revised and the income of married couples be made exempt up to $2,000 and of single persons up to $1,200. That is long past due, and we hope that the Minister of National Revenue meant what he said when he said that we would have a reduction of fifty per cent in our taxes.
The seriousness of the drought problem is well known to all Canadians, and during the last election campaign every political party promised its full support to irrigation. That is the one thing upon which we were and still are united. However, it remains for the party in power to show action in this respect and fulfil the election promises. We appreciate the steps already taken by the government in making a start on the St. Mary's-Milk river project, but let us go forward with all the power at our command to develop the irrigation projects.
I have another subject of paramount importance not only to the people of southern Alberta but to the people of Canada as a whole, namely, the trans-Canada highway. Canada requires an adequate highway system built around a hard surface trans-Canada highway equal to any one of the many excellent transcontinental highways in the United States. Otherwise Canada stands to lose her fair share of the tourist trade. This matter has received a great deal of attention by many

The Address-Mr. Wylie
of the citizens and organizations in and around Medicine Hat. We feel that adequate highways connecting one part of Canada with another are as essential in this day and age as railroads were in the early days of the west.
The dominion government recognized its responsibility in the building of railroads. Extension grants have been made to railways ever since confederation and many lines were built by government funds, because we were told our national economy required it.
During the war the dominion government expended large sums of money in the development of airports. The dominion government has never committed itself to a programme of highway construction; the only effort made by the government has been in the form of relief projects to create employment. I contend that roads, as public works and essential means of communication, should not be relegated to the status of relief projects. Neither railroads nor airports have been constructed in this manner, and roads are just as essential to-day to the welfare and economic development of Canada as are railroads or airports.
In Alberta we have some very good highways that are so located that they will make very fine feeder lines to connect with the trans-Canada. No. 1 highway is not in the best of shape at present, no doubt owing to the fact that the provincial government is waiting to see what developments are going to be made by the dominion government. Past experience has taught us that many provincial governments are not financially able to reconstruct highways of such high standards through sparsely populated areas, and if we depend on the provinces to build such a highway system it is not likely that it will ever be completed.
The demand for good roads from the populated areas is so great that every province is kept busy trying to satisfy the urgent demand made upon it. It is also apparent that no uniform type of highway will be constructed across Canada if the matter is left entirely in the hands of the individual provinces. Briefly, I might mention why the dominion government should take an active interest in the development of an adequate highway system. It would foster and encourage communication between the several provinces of our dominion with a view to developing a national spirit. It would attract United States tourists and thus enable us to capitalize on the favourable advertising we have received during the past six years. Tourist traffic from the United States affects the pocketbook of every Canadian citizen. One of the finest exports we have to offer the United States is our scenery, our hunting and our fishing. It could be worth
hundreds of millions of dollars to Canada. Prior to the war the tourist business had been developed into one of our largest industries, and it can be developed into our largest industry, out of which every man, woman and child in this country will receive some benefit either directly or indirectly.
In his speech the other night the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) mentioned the tourist traffic and said this:
Situated as we are, the tourist industry is of vital importance.
It is just as important to us in the west. Then he went on to show the number of tourists who had entered through the port of Windsor. In 1945 almost five and a half millions of United States tourists entered through the port of Windsor. That means a lot to the economy of any country.
Large sums have been [DOT] spent in laying out across our dominion one of the finest systems of national parks in the world; but in most instances there are no adequate highways upon which motorists may reach them, and there is definitely no system connecting these parks. One would almost think they were created only for the people living in the immediate vicinity. Our national parks compare favourably with, and some surpass, all other parks in North America. In addition, people will seek cooler places to spend vacations during hot weather if they 'have good highways over which to drive. We have been assured by experts on tourist travel from the United States that the tourist traffic is governed entirely by the type of roads supplied by Canada. People naturally drive north to reach a cooler climate during the summer months, and if our roads are comparable with those south of the United States boundary they would continue on to Canada and spend their vacations here. Tourist traffic from the United States is so important to our national economy that our highway, system should become a national project.
Of all the peoples of the world the citizens of the United States are the most travel-minded, and the opportunity presented to Canadians should be fostered and assisted in every way possible by the Dominion government. The proposals involve a change of policy in so far as the dominion government is concerned, but the matter is of such vital importance to our national welfare that I believe all the pressure possible should be brought to bear to ensure our so-called progressive country being provided with an
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny

adequate highway system which will be not only a credit to Canada but a great national asset enriching every citizen.
In closing, may I say that in the past we have always been told that the reason why the irrigation projects had not been completed is lack of money; but surely in view of the hundreds of millions of dollars given and lent, also credits to other, nations, it should not be asking too much to ask the government to spend a few million dollars on our own people to develop our own country. Abundant production and the successful distribution of goods constitute our greatest assurance against any inflation policy.

I cannot see the value of the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Agriculture engaging in a verbal duel in the House of Commons, and taking up three or four hours' time in doing so-not that I am complaining about that at all. But I cannot see the value of their telling the farmer what he shall do in connection with seeding because, after all, in the last analysis, the farmer is going to make his own decision as to how much grain he will sow. I have lived among farmers and have done some farming in my lifetime, and I have yet to know a farmer who goes to Hansard to find what the Minister of Agriculture had to say, before he pulls out his seed drill in the springtime.
Every farmer has to develop his own farming practice and his own farming unit. He has to put in the acreage which will fit in With his plans. Whatever the Minister of Agriculture may say, and no matter how the leader of the opposition may contradict the minister, these circumstances will not make any difference so far as making a decision as to how many acres of wheat are to be sown is concerned.
But I know what will make a difference. If we want to have greater wheat production or grain production of any kind, then I submit that there is only one way in which we can get that greater production. Apart altogether from the weather, we must provide a price which will establish a motive for the farmers to produce grain. I do. not know exactly what the price policy of the leader of the opposition is, although he did speak twice in. the debate. Unfortunately, however, in his second speech he usually contradicts what he says in his first one. But it seems to me that he advocates a price of $1.80; and so that hon. members will not think I am making it up, I shall quote from Hansard. At page 275 we find these words of the leader of the opposition:
In the meantime I would change the stupid policy which keeps the price of our export wheat 40 or 50 cents below the world price, and either fix it at $1.80 instead of $1.55, or let the world price prevail until the shortage is corrected.
Let me point out that the leader of the opposition has described as a stupid policy one which keeps the price of wheat 40 or 50 cents below the world price. If one adds 40 or 50 cents to $1.55 he finds that it brings the price up to $1.95 or $2.05. Yet the leader of the opposition advocates $1.80, which is still below the world price, and is therefore still a stupid policy.
That is only your say so.

Well, I am reading it from Hansard. Even though the farmer is in-

terested in the ceiling price or the highest price that he can get for his wheat-and that is undeniable-I believe that through bitter experience he has learned that it is far more important for him to know the lowest guaranteed price he may expect to get. He has seen times when wheat jumped up to $2 a bushel, and other times when it has fallen to 20 cents. So that the farmer wants to know, first, the guaranteed price the government is willing to give for the next four or five or more years.
I believe, if we want to get greater grain production, we might use a simple formula, namely that of letting the present ceiling price become the floor price. Under those conditions the farmers will produce grain for the next four or five years-that is, if they are sure that they are not going to produce at a low price.
It is far more important to have a guaranteed price of $1.55 as a floor than to let the wheat price go up to $1.80 or $2, and put the farmer back into a speculative market, and take a chance on' it again.
Another obstacle that can be removed from production is the matter of gasoline prices. Eariy in this session I took occasion to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) whether he would reconsider the order which has been made permitting an increase of two cents a gallon on the price of gasoline. His answer was that the matter has been given consideration, and that he was not prepared to make any further promise.
I know the farmers are dissatisfied with that price increase. I do not think I can find better words to emphasize that dissatisfaction than to read a letter, a copy of which was signed by over a hundred farmers in my constituency, and sent to me. This is addressed to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada, and says: .
Sir:
As a fanner trying to help feed .a hungry world I wish to vigorously protest against the proposed advance in the price of gasoline, as it is another brake on the wheels of industry and a deterrent to agricultural production. If we are to avoid the hazards of inflation it seems to me that the government should be the last to countenanace the proposed advance of the oil corporations who have made huge profits all through the war years, and are well able to stand on their own feet in the transition to normal times.
The farmer of western Canada has been asked to bolster international good will by selling his wheat greatly below world prices. Bacon and other products over a bargain counter.
The Canadian consumer is getting his flour greatly below world wheat value and the eastern feeder of live stock is being subsidized at the western farmer's expense.

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
If I have anything left over in a good year the income tax agent is on hand to attach the money that I have been trying for years to get to improve my humble home and surroundings, the remodeling of which is long past due. Now the government wants me to help out the poor oil baron. This is about the last straw. Have the legislators forgotten the .recent kick in the pants they received when they tried to raise the tariff on certain steel products. The western farmer has not.
The sit-down strike is in progress and will soon reach disastrous proportions if something is not done and done quickly.
The Minister of Finance did not lay before the house an accounting of why it is necessary to permit oil companies to raise their prices. He did mention a subsidy, and made it appear as if the western provinces were the only ones receiving subsidies. As a matter of fact, in the last year the government spent over S103 million in subsidies; and I state, therefore, that $3,500,000 to western farmers does not loom up quite so large in comparison.
I wish to mention another obstacle which should be removed in connection with implements for war veterans. There is a certain class of war veteran who is not able to obtain the farm implements which he needs because he cannot take advantage of the provisions of the land act. I refer to the veteran who, instead of buying land under the act, has bought it with his own money or has had land given to him, perhaps by his father. Under the act he is not eligible for a grant with which to buy farm equipment and therefore is under a handicap. I hope this situation will be remedied.
I should like to point out to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does not operate to the advantage of all farmers. I mentioned last year the matter I have in mind and hoped there would be some change made, but apparently nothing has yet been done. I have a letter which I received to-day from the deputy minister of agriculture in connection with an area in my constituency which was damaged by hail. One sentence in that letter reads:
Township 29-20-W1, R.M. of Mossey river, was found by the board of review to have an average wheat yield of 8-3 bushels per acre; therefore, the board of review declared the township ineligible.
There have been many areas damaged by hail where the wheat crop averaged over eight bushels per acre, and therefore the particular township would not be eligible for prairie farm assistance. I would point out to the minister that it is almost impossible to find an area damaged by hail where there will be a large, wide belt of damage. This act may be suitable for relieving drought conditions,
but it certainly does not work in the case of hail damage. I believe some provision should be made to provide for relief on an individual basis, say from section to section rather than from township to township. Then the individual farmer whose crops had been damaged by hail would not have to depend upon his neighbour's crops being damaged in order to obtain assistance from the government. It would almost appear that if there had been a little more hail in this particular township the farmers would have been better off, because then the average yield would have been .3 bushels per acre less and they would have then been eligible for prairie farm assistance.
I should like to touch briefly upon the matter of industrial production. This subject has been covered by other hon. members, but I wish to say that fhe government is going to have to do some tall explaining to the people of this country. At the present time there are over a quarter of a million unemployed. There is also a great shortage of consumer'goods; houses are needed at a time when materials for building those houses exist in Canada. I would not be saying this if I did not feel that the government had promised the people of this country full employment. As was pointed out the other day by an hon. member, before the election took place we saw large signs nailed up on fences and telephone posts saying, "Jobs for all" in letters about six feet high.
I refrained from saying anything about this during the last session because I felt the government should be given a breathing spell after the war in order to readjust industry and put things in order. But in my opinion they have had sufficient time to get the wheels of industiy turning. If they are not able to provide full employment when there is such a shortage of goods of all kinds, when there is such a need all over the world for the products that we can produce, what prospect is there for full employment, let us say five years from now?
I feel a little apprehensive about the whole matter because I am afraid we are back on that downhill run that we took in 1930. Unless the government can figure out some way to make private industry provide jobs for all, then I think the only alternative is to plan for full employment and full production under public enterprise as was done during the war.
In conclusion, I wish to touch upon a question that was brought up in this house during last session and again at this session. I hope this is not a controversial matter because it does not enter into party politics. I refer to the displaced persons and refugees in
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
.COMMONS
Europe. As a member nation of UNO we have a responsibility to discharge. As a member of the British commonwealth of nations we have a tradition to live up to. The responsibility that we have as a member nation of the united nations is clearly set out in the charter of the united nations. I intend to quote directly from that charter in order that I may have for the plea I intend to make a basis that is authentic. One of the objectives set out in the preamble is:
To reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small.
I agree heartily with that. Then in article 1, section 2, these words appear:
To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples.
Again I am glad .to agree with that. Then in section 3 of the same article there are these words:
To achieve international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character.
These quotations appear in the charter of the united nations which has been endorsed by this house and which has received, I believe, the whole-hearted support of every hon. member. It is upon these three quotations that I wish to base my plea. I do not intend to go over this question of displaced persons and refugees because it has been fully explained in this house. I only want to point out that there are a great many of these unfortunate people in Europe who have to turn to someone- for moral and material assistance. I do not know to whom they can better turn than to a member of the united nations. I do not think we will back up on the position we took when we endorsed the united nations charter, when we undertook to extend democratic and human rights, the rights of freedom and liberty to all the peoples of the earth.
While UNRRA is doing a splendid job in Europe, it. has certain limitations as far as displaced persons and refugees are concerned. The provisions governing UNRRA state plainly that it is to deal with constituted nations. That is, the organization is set up in such a way that all nations contribute what they can, and then those who need assistance receive that assistance through the regular channels of their governments. But we must realize that there are perhaps several million people in Europe to-day who cannot truthfully say that they have a nation, who because of their political or religious beliefs or for some other reason find themselves not only

homeless but nationless. UNRRA is limited in what it can do for those people. It is true that the Red Cross has come in to fill the gap and has done a wonderful job, a job which will be remembered for generations to come, but that organization also has its limitations ; it cannot do all that it would like to do.
As I said, we have a responsibility as a member nation of the united ns.tions. We also have a tradition to uphold as a member of the British commonwealth of nations. The tradition that has been built up in the British commonwealth of nations, especially in Great Britain, the mother of the commonwealth, is one which will go down in history, not only for generations but for centuries to come. One of the reasons for the greatness of Great Britain and the British commonwealth of ' nations has been and remains that spirit of tolerance, that insistence on the other fellow's rights as well as your own, and a readiness to help out people who have become political or religious refugees. I think, if we accept the premise that all peoples on this earth have a right to believe as they please, to think what they like and say what they like, then we cannot but agree that the greatness of a nation is measured by the degree of tolerance and the degree of freedom and the lack of discrimination that it shows among all its peoples. I believe that Great Britain occupies the place in world history and in the minds of the peoples of the world that she does to-day chiefly because of this one quality, which has been her greatest quality, the spirit of tolerance and the spirit of freedom which it has been willing to extend to all people. As a member of the British commonwealth of nations, Canada, I believe, can take a lead in* this matter.
I have said once before, and I repeat, that we should take our share of refugees into this country if we can possibly do so. I wish to make it very clear, as I have on other occasions, that I am not at all interested and have no wish to drag into this discussion any political implications. If we are going to help the people of Europe in a moral or material way I believe that we shall help them best by allowing them to settle their own political differences among themselves, because by the very nature of things we are too far removed to understand all the intricacies of their political differences. So that I say I am not looking at this question at all from a political angle but purely from a humanitarian point of view as one who voted for the adoption of the united nations charter.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
I believe that we can help by accepting into this country our share of refugees. I know there is a hesitancy on the part of the government to do this, perhaps for two reasons. There is the fear that it may have political repercussions because all types of opinions have been expressed on this matter, and there is also hesitancy because of the unemployment situation in this country. I have letters on file from the immigration department in which they express doubt whether it would be good policy to bring in people when our own employment situation is not of the best.
But I wish to make a concrete proposal to the government, in which I believe there will be no political implications and which will involve no danger of putting anyone in this country out of a job. The suggestion is not original with me; it was made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum). It is this, that we bring to this country, let us say to start with, 10,000 children of displaced persons and refugees, who from the very nature of things are the most innocent and most unfortunate victims of the war and its aftermath. Let people in this country who are willing and in a position to do so, take these children into their homes and bring them up as young Canadians. Let them stay here at least for a while. There may be some who after staying here for a number of years may apply for permission to remain permanently, and I have no doubt that will be true of the great majority. There may be others who, for personal reasons, or sentimental attachments, may wish, after staying here for a number of years, to go back to Europe. Both of these groups will be of great help to this country. Those who stay here will have been brought up in the spirit of Canadianism, and will have grown up under our laws and will be perhaps the most grateful type of Canadian that we can have, because they will realize that we have come to their help when they needed it most. Those who go back would also be a great help to us, because they will be ambassadors of good will of the very best type. Can one imagine any better people to go back to Europe, perhaps to those dark spots where the light of freedom and democracy has not yet penetrated, than young people who have grown up in this country and learned something of the ways of tolerance and freedom in a democracy and of the things we hold dear in this country? Back in Europe they can preach the gospel of friendship to Canada. I cannot imagine any better kind of advertising or any better ambassadors of good will that we could have. It would be far better than sending out 63260-23
Canadians who have grown up into adult life in this country, not knowing European ways and not being able to compare or contrast conditions in the two countries. Therefore I make the suggestion that we allow near relatives or close friends in this country, who are in a financial position to do so, to bring in children of displaced persons or refugees and give them a home and an education and a Canadian upbringing, something that will be for the benefit both of this country and the continent of Europe.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a word. I do not intend to continue the discussion that has taken place in this debate. I have not spoken on the motion and am therefore entitled to speak at this time. All I wish to say, however, is a word to hon. members concerning the motion that is now before the house; a word in relation thereto which has an immediate bearing on the evolution of our parliamentary practice.
The motion that is now before the house is:
That the following address he presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada: May it please Your Excellency:
We His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both houses.of parliament.
Hon. members will see that the motion is simply a word of thanks to His Excellency for the speech which His Excellency addressed to both houses in opening the present session of parliament, nothing more and nothing less. It is identical in style and words with the address which over many years has been employed at Westminster.
I do not know what hon. gentlemen opposite are laughing at; I am simply stating something that is wholly obvious. Amendments have been presented to this address on three occasions in the course of the debate, each expressing a certain want of confidence in the government. All three have been rejected. The house has discussed those amendments to the address and all of them have been rejected. There remains now only the motion which is a word of thanks to the governor general for his courtesy in presenting the house with a speech which would enable it to open its proceedings-a word of thanks for that particular courtesy expressed in the form of an address, this being the appropriate manner in which to approach the sovereign or his representative.
The custom in the British house has been to adopt the address without any division. The earlier practice was to adopt the address



The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
without any previous amendment, being moved. The custom of adopting the address without amendment has altered' of recent years and amendments have from time to time been presented. But the parliamentary practice, generally, has been to adopt the address, without any division for both houses to adopt it unanimously.
I widi to quote to the house certain authorities in support of the statement I have just made. I have here "On Parliamentary Government in England," by Alpheus Todd, volume II, second edition. At page 363 hon. members will find the following:
It has now become .a well-established rule, to regard the speech from the throne, and the address 'in reply thereto, as reciprocal acts of courtesy between the crown and the houses of parliament, and the address itself as the unanimous and respectful expression of the deference with which the house should receive the first communication of the session from the sovereign, and as pledging the house to nothing, save the serious consideration of the matters referred to therein.
I quote from page 364:
Accordingly, it has gradually become the practice to refrain from moving an amendment to the address in answer to the royal speech, "unless some great political objects were in view, and likely to ibe attained"; or, unless some assertion were made in the address to which the opposition found it impossible to assent.
That has reference to the amendment to the address. But, as I have just said, the old custom of not even having an amendment to the address moved has altered in the course of the years and amendments have from time to time been brought forward. Once one or more amendments have been brought forward and rejected', the house comes to have only the original motion before it, which motion is in the nature of a reciprocal courtesy, a word of thanks to the representative of the King- that is to say, in this country-or in Great Britain to the King himself.
I refer now to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, third edition, at page 191:
It is felt that the questions mentioned in the speech can be more conveniently discussed when the house is in full possession of all the information necessary to the consideration of any important subject. Sometimes, however, the house may be called upon to express its opinions at length, and to vote on an amendment to, the address, which involves the fate of the government of the day. But under ordinary circumstances the desire is to pass the address with as little delay as 'possible, and to confine the debate to a general review of the policy of the government, without taking up those specific subjects on which the necessary information is not yet before the house. It is felt desirable, whenever practicable, to allow the address to pas6 without a division and "be in point of fact the unanimous and respectful expression of the

deference with which the houses receive the first communication of the session" from the sovereign or her representatitve.
I come now to a much more recent authority, namely, Campion, well recognized authority in the United Kingdom. The volume from which I am about to quote is entitled, "An Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons." I must first quote from page vii of the preface:
This book was projected merely 'as a manual of first-aid for new members, but with the friendly connivance and encouragement of my publisher its scope has been considerably enlarged. It now aims at presenting a complete account of the procedure of the House of Commons, on a scale midway between the official Manual of Procedure and May's Parliamentary Practice, with fuller explanations and illustrations than the former and in a shorter and more readily accessible shape than the latter.
On page 83 of this volume will be found a section which deals with the King's speech, "Debate upon the Address in answer to the King's Speech." I should like to quote from that paragraph:
The address in answ-er to the king's speech is moved and seconded by two members selected by the Prime Minister, one a representative of a borough,-
That is in England, of course.
*-the other of a county, constituency . . .
Formerly the address was framed to follow the king's speech paragraph by paragraph, but it is now moved in the form of a short expression of thanks. The debate, which follows, normally falls into two parts:	(1) a general
debate upon the policy of the government as outlined in the speech, and (2) debate on the amendments moved by the opposition, advocating alternative policies, usually expressed in the form of regret for the omission from the speech of the policies advocated. Some five days are by agreement usually devoted to this debate. At its conclusion the address is voted and ordered to be presented to His Majesty "by such members of the house as are of His Majesty's privy council, or of His Majesty's household."
I have looked through several other authorities and cannot find any which take issue with the statement that it is correct parliamentary practice for the house to approve unanimously the motion to thank the sovereign or his representative for having at the beginning of a session come to meet the members of the two houses, to open their proceedings by a speech from the throne.

May I ask the Prime
Minister a question? Does he then regard the passage of the address, without division, as an expression of confidence in the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Most certainly not.

The Address

Mr. Mackenzie King
That is the whole point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I wish to make that clear. Nor does the passage of the address without division commit any member to anything expressed in the address. An amendment affords an opportunity to take exception to what appears or does not appear in the speech from the throne and to the government's policy, but when amendments which have been proposed are rejected and there is nothing left but the simple expression of thanks to His Majesty or His Majesty's representative for having come to parliament and opened its proceedings, it certainly places the Commons in an anomalous position vis-avis the crown to refuse to thank His Majesty or His Majesty's representative for that act of courtesy.

I believe the general
impression here is that voting approval of the address is voting confidence in. the government and its policies. That is the general impression in the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That was my
reason for intervening in the debate at this stage. As leader of the house I have a responsibility to the house in matters of this kind and for that reason I speak at the present time. I should regret to see in this parliament, in the evolution of our parliamentary practice, any course that would depart, either in the letter or in the spirit, from what is obviously the right course of procedure to be followed in relations between members of the House of Commons and the sovereign or his representative. Consequently, I have brought this matter to the attention of the house tonight. Probably I must hold myself in part responsible for what has happened where there has been a departure from this practice. Between 1935 and 1940 there were no divisions on the motion in reply to the speech from the throne, the address each year was carried unanimously. Between 1940 and 1945 there were divisions. The record discloses that the house divided on the motion, or rather, that the motion was passed "on division". I believe that arose because a certain number of members on those occasions rose in their places or called "on division", and the Speaker was obliged to record a division. I am perfectly sure that the hon. members, in so doing, did not realize that what in fact they were doing was to request that the representative of the crown be not thanked for having come to open formally the proceedings of parliament.
So far as the British house is concerned, I have looked through the records of the last ten years, and I find that while there have 63260-231
been amendments to this address, which were debated and rejected, no division has been recorded on the motion to thank the crown. There have been some occasions, both in England and also in earlier years in this parliament, on which there have been divisions, but that has been for some exceptional reason.
It is for hon. members to take whatever course they wish. I do not desire to limit the house in the course it may wish to take on the motion now to be put by His Honour the Speaker, but I believe that the correct practice is that, now all amendments have been rejected and disposed of, the house should unanimously agree to thank His Excellency for the speech which he addressed to both houses in opening the present session. May I make it clear that, this being done, it will be understood, and must be understood, that the house is not thereby giving any vote of confidence in the government. The confidence which the government enjoys has been shown on the three motions in the nature of amendments that have already been before the house, debated, and rejected.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, yes. So far as this motion is concerned, however, it is an act of courtesy in relation entirely to the sovereign or rather to his representative in Canada, and not an expression one way or the other of the confidence which hon. members may or may not have in the government.
The right hon. gentleman has studied the question. Perhaps he will tell the chamber what was the practice and what actually happened during the-time he had the honour of leading the; opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When I had the honour of leading the opposition between 1931 and 1935 some members did, I recall, rise on one occasion and there was a recorded division. I have already said that I am prepared to share responsibility for an error in procedure that has developed in that way. But now that I see the correct procedure as clearly as I do, I feel it my duty to bring it to the attention of the house.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

On division.
Main motion (Mr. Viau) agreed to on division.
Right Hon, W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): The first business after the address has been agreed to is for this house to order that the address be engrossed and

That the address be engrossed and presented to His Excellency the Governor General by such members of the house as are of the honourable the privy council.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: BUTTER STORAGE AND SUPPLY, MONTREAL AREA
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES-PATRICIA BAY-SEA ISLAND FARES
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	On August 1, 1945, Trans-Canada Air Lines licence which authorized the transport of through traffic to Victoria was amended to authorize the company to carry local traffic
Questions

between Vancouver and Victoria. Effective August 7, 1945, the fare of S3 one way and $5.40 for the round trip was established by T.C.A. for such local traffic. Air transport board Order No. 2 directed that these fares be increased to $5 one way and $10 round trip. The increase became effective January 1, 1946.
This action by the air transport board was taken as a result of. a complaint made by Canadian Pacific Air Lines that the T.C.A. fares of $3 one way and $5.40 return were not just and reasonable.
The facts as found by the air transport board were as follows:
Prior to August 1945 C.P.A.L. and its predecessors had been, for a considerable period, the air carriers authorized to provide the local service between Victoria and Vancouver and they had in the past, and still did carry the bulk of the traffic.
A most careful scrutiny by the board and its economic experts established beyond question that the rate of $5 one way, which was the rate being charged by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, did little more than barely cover the actual cost of operation as a local service and that C.P.A.L. was conducting its said operation on a sound and economic basis.
On the other hand, T.C.A. was operating a trunk line service on a basis of only two trips daily each way, in regard to which the local service between Vancouver and Victoria was merely incidental. In effect, the number of seats available on T.C.A. for the local service was entirely dependent on the number reserved for through traffic. In the event that all seats were utilized by T.C.A. for through traffic, there would be none for local traffic. It was, therefore, obvious that the considerations *which applied to T.C.A. rates were substantially different from those which governed the operations of C.P.A.L. Having regard to all the circumstances, it appeared to be clearly unsound to permit T.C.A. who could not carry all the traffic, or even any of it, if all its seats were occupied by through passengers, to operate on the basis of a rate which was substantially below the actual cost of operation of the purely local service in question. Had T.C.A. been able to handle all the traffic that offered, different considerations would have applied.
Section 5 (1) of the air transport board regulations respecting commercial air services provides that air carriers must furnish transportation upon reasonable request and must provide safe and adequate service, equipment and facilities. Quite obviously, to provide a

service which complies with all these requirements, it is essential that the air carrier receive a reasonable rate of remuneration. It would have been unreasonable and unfair to require C.P.A.L. to reduce its rates, with the possible result that the service would have been discontinued. As the communities served were primarily dependent upon that company for the local air services in question, the board found that the complaint of C.P.A.L. was justified and under the authority contained in its regulations the board ordered the change in rate hereinbefore referred to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR APRIL 10 AS JACK MINER NATIONAL WILD LIFE DAY

speechtext:
Mr. J. R. MacNICOL (Davenport) moved the second reading of bill No. 2, respecting the Jack Miner National Wild Life Day.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I feel very humble in moving second reading of a bill which has to do with the perpetuation of the memory of a great Canadian, one who was recognized everywhere as the .pioneer conservator of wild life not only in, Canada but throughout America, and as the greatest naturalist on this continent.
A few days ago I read an article in a magazine which classed the late Jack Miner, who was a great pioneer, with other great pioneers, other men who blazed' name and fame across the skies. His name appeared alongside names of men like Sir Henry Bessemer, who invented a process in connection with the production of steel, one which revolutionized steel production throughout the world. Then there was Luther Burbank, who was a great horticulturist. In the list was Louis Pasteur whose name is known throughout the world, and who has been recognized as a great French scientist. There was Graham Bell, who invented the telephone; Thomas A. Edison; Doctor Grenfell; Doctor Banting; Lord Kelvin; Remington, who invented the typewriter; the Wright brothers, who invented the aeroplane; Ford, who was the pioneer in low-priced motor cars, and Jack Miner himself.
This lists twelve great men; and as a Canadian I am proud that, through his great work, Jack Miner earned the right to have his name alongside the names of those other great pioneers. So many have spoken to me in support of the bill that I know I shall not have to speak at length at this time. On the other hand, so many have asked questions respecting its significance that I feel I should answer those questions as they have come to me.
Some have asked how the bill came to be introduced-who it was who suggested it. Well, this is the second bill I have introduced in this connection. The first was introduced in 1941. only in Canada, but in America. It is situated in a perfect garden country, a fact which must be known to all who have been there. These buses turned at the main corner of the town of Kingsville for the purpose of going north for a distance of a mile or so to the sanctuary created by the late Jack Miner.
One of the men standing at the corner was Mr. Arthur Allen who, on several occasions, had proposed to the Kingsville council that they take steps to set apart a day. He had suggested that they should choose April 10, Jack Miner's birthday, as a day on which not only the children from Detroit, but those from all other parts of Ontario and the United States might visit the sanctuary. That is the origin of the bill. The idea was suggested to me while I was there, with the result that in the following year I introduced a bill. However, on account of the war, it was suggested to me that any action in connection with the bill might be deferred until after the war. I was glad to comply with the suggestion; I am always happy to cooperate if I can.
I know there is nothing I can add to either the name or the fame of Jack Miner. All the great men in America have done that; they have left nothing for anyone else to add. Therefore I shall not try.
I have been asked what states have wild life days. Perhaps I should explain that I have received literature from the United States. A tremendous amount of it has come to my desk, from all sorts of organizations. That to which I shall direct the attention of the house is the literature which reached me from that great American organization known as the National Wild Life Federation in the United States. From that literature I learn that it was the late President, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, a very great friend of our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who originated the idea in that country. I might say, in passing, that it is a blessing the President and our Prime Minister were such good friends during those days of struggle through which we have passed. I believe that our Prime Minister's influence with the President was most helpful in those negotiations which took place between the United States and the British empire.
It was in 1938 that the late President set apart the first day of spring as wild life day in the United States. They set apart the week of March 21-and had I known that . when I drafted this bill, instead of mentioning a single day I would have inserted the words "the week of April 10". Some people have asked, "How are you going to hold to April 10, when it might fall on a Saturday or Sunday, and in that way would not be effective in the schools?" I note that in some of the states this difficulty has been overcome by setting apart a week or a month and, if this bill is accepted, the necessary change could be made in this direction by way of amendment.
In the United States they have what is known as national wild life week. This is the statement made by the National Wild Life Federation:
National wild life week, originally proclaimed by President Roosevelt in 1938 as a .period in which Americans should give thoughtful consideration to wild life, its restoration and preservation, will begin this year on March 21, the first day of spring, the National Wild Life Federation has announced.
Sponsored by the federation, wild life week is featured by many kinds of educational activities carried on by various organizations, groups .and agencies .affiliated with the federation. In addition there will be lectures,- radio talks, newspaper stories, school programmes, etc., throughout the country, devoted to an intelligent approach to conservation of soil, water, fields and forests as well as wild life.
I am assured by the Miner foundation that they, and the organizations with which they are closely associated in Canada and whose work in connection with wild life conservation they sponsor, will supply all the literature required, and I have no doubt that they will carry out this undertaking.
Most of the southern states in the United States have adopted wild life weeks. They have followed the federal government's programme and have selected the week of March 21. In the south the season is much more advanced; in fact the geese and ducks all left for the north early in March. A little different programme is followed in the northern states, and I shall refer to Ohio as an example. Arbour day, which as I remember is on a Friday, in April, is selected and the week in which that day falls is set aside as wild life week. I should like to read two or three paragraphs from a proclamation which was issued by the state of Ohio in 1943. These read:	t
Whereas, for the past four years, the entire month of April has been set .aside as conservation month in Ohio, thus kindling anew the interest of our citizens in all phases of conservation, and	*
National Wild Lije Day

Whereas, the teaching of conservation in the schools of Ohio has been commended in a joint programme of the state department of education and the Ohio division of conservation.
And further down:
Now, therefore, I, John W. Bricker, governor of the state of Ohio, do hereby appoint and designate the week of April 12 to 16 as conservation week in the schools of Ohio and Friday, April 16, -as arbour and bird day and ask a general observance by all citizens of the state of the entire month of April as conservation month.
I understand that the state of Michigan takes arbour day as the pivotal day in their wild life conservation week. I shall not take time to give details of what that state does, but it is along the lines of what I have just read. There is nothing new in a wild life day or a wild life week, because as far as I know it is general throughout the states of the United States. Therefore I feel the time has come when Canada should do the same.
The United States does not have an outstanding conservationist or wild life advocate like the late Jack Miner was, and it seems to me that April 10, which is the anniversary of the birthday of this great wild life conservationist and this great naturalist, would be a fitting day to include in a wild life week, or to be set aside as a wild life day as the bill provides. There are many days in Canada that are fairly generally observed. There is a day for tuberculosis; there is apple day which is the Boy Scout day and which is a national day throughout Canada; there is fire prevention week and so on. All of these are good, and to set aside April 10 as a wild life conservation day would be a new thing in Canada and would place us in the same position as the United States. The bill says a day, but it can be amended, to week of April 10.
During this period speeches could be delivered over the radio and all those interested could spread far and wide the benefits which would accrue to this country from conservation along almost any lines, and, in this particular case, wild life conservation.
It has been suggested to me that perhaps we would be interfering with the educational systems of the provinces. The provinces are supreme in educati anal matters and the federal government cannot interfere. I do not feel that there would be any interference because there would be no compulsion upon any provincial department of education to follow the provisions of this bill. I presume they would do just the same as is done in the various states in the United States. The departments of education in all the provinces are thoroughly alive to the great value of conservation in all

lines, and, in this case, the conservation of wild life. I do not fear any difficulty in that regard, although it is not for me to say.
I was a very close friend of the late Jack Miner. I often visited his sanctuary, and it is a little difficult for me to speak because I think of his lovely blue eyes and his lovely face which showed by its lines his love, not only for wild life but for humanity. Quite often when I was there children would come, and I used to stand back and watch the faces of the kiddies when they looked at Jack Miner. He was an institution to them and busloads of children would come to see him. They would show him their bird houses and he would pat this 'one on the head and that one on the back. I can see- their lovely eyes and their lovely countenances looking at his.
He was a great conservator; he devoted his whole life to conservation. The hon. members from Essex county know this quite well. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), who previously represented an Essex constituency in the provincial house, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) are all familiar with the work of this great pioneer, perhaps more so than other members in the house. I like to think of a pioneer being a man who blazes the way, who is not just a follower; a man who steps out and puts his name before the world. That is what Jack Miner did, and everything he did was done for Canada.
1 have received many communications and I think I should refer to one or two. One was from the London Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. I often heard Jack Miner say, "If I can teach a child to make an outdoor birdcage, I have made a conservator of wild life." That was a great thought; that was his life, as opposed to useless destruction. Wild life means so much to this country besides sport; it can contribute so much in the way of food, and its preservation is of the utmost importance. I also had-a very warm letter from Colonel E. S. Wigle, one of the oldest residents and1 a member of one of the pioneer families in that part of Ontario. He warmly approves the bill.
I also had a letter from a leading departmental store in Windsor, the C. H. Smith departmental store. Although I am not familiar with the store itself, I understand it is a very large store. I believe the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) told me it was tlie largest store in Windsor. They are going to use their big show-windows, I am informed, to present to passers-by a demonstration of the value of wild life conservation. I think it is fine for a great merchant to use the show-

National Wild Lije Day
windows of his store to interest people in wild life conservation. It is an indication that people are thinking of more than merely profit.
I also had a letter from the Chrysler Corporation, of Detroit, Michigan; everyone knows who they are; also one from Doctor Perkins Bull, a great conservator himself. If I may digress for a moment, Doctor Bull has gathered together, in my opinion, the greatest collection of early pioneer farm equipment used in Canada that I have ever seen anywhere. He has it housed in a museum which is part of a school at Brampton, where there must, be at least one-quarter of a million dollars worth of material. I appreciate his letter very much, coming from a pioneer himself.
I also received one from the Ottawa Humane Society and one from the National Parks Association of Canada, from which I quote this paragraph:
*Canada is so far "behind the United States in practical wild life conservation that it could *almost .be said that we have not even made a start officially.
I think the Department of Mines and Resources has made a start and I wish to compliment the department on the distance it has gone in that regard. I am looking for great things along that line from the new Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), because he comes from a province where there is much to be accomplished in conservation of wild life and summers in a very great park in Manitoba, Riding Mountain park, in which there is much wild life protected. So that I look for a lot from him in the development of wild life conservation.
I quote another paragraph from the same letter:
The National Parks Association have a bulletin awaiting its turn at the printer's stressing the Americans' effort a.nd many of this 5,000 *edition should be in the mail before April 10.
The National Parks Association of Canada deserves unstinted credit and praise for going to the trouble of getting out and printing this bulletin. It is encouraging when you know that so many people are interested in promoting wild life conservation. Jack Miner was the pioneer in that field. There have been many others since and there were others during his time who have done a lot in that direction. I am looking at my friend the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), whose name I deliberately picked out as seconder of the bill because he is more familiar than many others are with the conservation of the Canada goose. He himself I believe has quite a sanctuary near Cochrane and when I go out that way again I will visit him. When
the geese leave Virginia and the Carolinas and Texas and Louisiana they fly north and cover six hundred miles the first day and then come down to rest. I believe it is the third day before they get to the sanctuary.
I have seen 50,000 geese at Jack Miner's sanctuary at Kingsville, and all through the years, Mr. Speaker, the Miner sanctuary has fed those geese. It takes many thousands of bushels of No. 1 com yearly to feed them.
I have watched his men on many occasions distributing the corn when the geese have gone out to the lake. The sanctuary covers a very large area, about four hundred acres altogether, but where the birds go is about twenty-five to thirty acres, ponds included, and the corn is distributed all around these. It is most interesting to watch them. I was thinking this afternoon, when I was told that this bill might come up, of the many occasions on which I have gone with Jack Miner to the little house he had amongst the trees. You had to reach it by a ladder and peep out through a peephole at the geese. They are bright and intelligent birds. Jack used to say they were the wisest of all wild life; in fact he did not call them wild. In order not to frighten the geese there were pieces of coloured glass hanging in the peep-hole in front of the people through which you could get a good look at them without their seeing you. I do not like to think when I go back there that I shall not have the pleasure of the company of that great pioneer.
I had another letter from the department of street railways, Detroit. I value this letter because that is a great organization. They have written me approving the bill. I also received a letter from the Canadian Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, Montreal, in which they warmly approve the bill. I quote this one paragraph from their letter:
In the matter pertaining to the Bill representing "National Bird Day"-
That is not the right name:
-I am pleased to state that our society appreciates the opportunity of concurring with you in your noble effort and may we hope that a favourable reception will be given your efforts.
I have another letter from a Windsor firm, Abbey Gray Limited, a motor car company, warmly approving the bill, and a very strong letter from the Essex county tourist association, signed by II. J. Lassaline, secretary-treasurer. I had the pleasure of meeting him at the Jack Miner sanctuary.
I have a clipping from the Globe and Mail, which quotes from the Calgary Herald, and I will read very briefly from it:
National Wild Life Day

Following this war there will be a great increase in the numbers of hunters and fishermen. Millions of young men who have learned the thrill of outdoor living will join the ranks of those older sportsmen who are already devotees of the rugged life. Pressure on wild life resources will be terrific. The result will be the virtual exhaustion of our game, unless game management can solve the problems of providing annual crops of game animals, birds and fish in sufficient amount to satisfy the demands of this army of sportsmen.
That is the purpose of the bill, that all sorts of sportsmen's organizations should do in Canada as similar bodies do in the United States. At their dinners or banquets in the week of April 10, in Canada, they should have speakers who will tell their members, and through their members the public, of the great value of wild life conservation all along the line. If we do that we shall preserve for right use the wild life in Canada.
Perhaps I might quote another paragraph of the letter from the National Parks Association. I ought to have quoted this before. This has reference to the United States:
As you know, they have 178 water fowl refuges totalling 3,415,542 acres supported by the sale in 1945 of 1,750,352 one-dollar duck stamps to hunters and -a few postage stamp collectors.
Since that time another 500,000 acres have been added to their wild fowl refuges. I do not know whether we have a tabulation of wild fowl refuges, but they now have 4,000,000 acres; and taking all their wild life, big game and wild fowl, they have altogether 13,600,000 acres. Speakers at various organizations should emphasize the necessity of Canada preserving some swamps and so forth. When the geese leave the Miner sanctuary I believe it takes them two days to get to the riding represented by the hon. member for Cochrane, and they go in thousands near the shores of James Bay, remaining there a week or ten days or more before flying to their nesting grounds in Baffin Land, Ungava and the Arctic islands. That is why I have referred to the hon. member for Cochrane as a conservationist. He is thoroughly familiar with the value of conservation.
I wish to say a word further with reference to Jack Miner. Among other titles, he had earned that of the great missionary of the air. He was the pioneer tagger of wild fowl. Others are now doing the same thing, and all credit to them, but he was the pioneer. That is the point I wish to emphasize above all others, and that is why so many honours have come to him. While I am on this point, let me give due credit to my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, who alone must have conferred upon Jack Miner the O.B.E. of which he was so justly proud. I have never 
seen anyone in my life so thrilled at receiving a title as Jack was when he received the O.B.E., and I may tell the Prime Minister that if at any time he. visits the sanctuary he will find above the big fireplace in the living room three pictures, one of Edison, one of Henry Ford and one of our Prime M inister.
